monster.name: Domestic Wonder [5.5e]

trait.name: Mechanical Determination
trait.text: If damage reduces the wonder to 0 Hit Points, it makes a Constitution saving throw with a DC of 5 plus the damage taken unless the damage is Lightning or from a Critical Hit. On a successful save, the wonder drops to 1 Hit Point instead.

trait.name: Wind-Up Operation
trait.text: The wonder has the Unconscious condition until another creature winds it with the wonder's unique key for 1 minute. Once wound, the wonder operates for 10 days or until a creature touches the wonder with its key as a Utilize action to deactivate it, after which the wonder has the Unconscious condition until it is wound again.

monster.description:
A Mechanical Wonder is a semi-autonomous object imbued with magical power. Mechanical Wonders vary greatly in size and form depending on their function. A Mechanical Wonder is a dormant object until activated. To activate a Mechanical Wonder, you must wind the wonder with a handheld key unique to that wonder. It takes 1 minute to wind a Mechanical Wonder. While you wind it, you must take the Utilize action each turn. Once wound, a Mechanical Wonder remains activated for the duration specified in the wonder's description below.
This bipedal wonder is designed to assist with household duties. It vaguely resembles whatever species its creator used as inspiration. An activated domestic wonder uses the Domestic Wonder stat block. The wonder is an ally to you and your allies. In combat, the wonder shares your Initiative count, but it takes its turn immediately after yours. It obeys your verbal commands (no action required by you). If you don't issue any, it takes the Dodge action and uses its movement to avoid danger. The domestic wonder is destroyed if it drops to 0 Hit Points.
Source: Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn p. 245, Forgotten Realms: Heroes of Faerûn p. 134

monster.name: Flying Wonder [5.5e]

trait.name: Increased Carrying Capacity
trait.text: The wonder can carry up to 100 pounds.

trait.name: Wind-Up Operation
trait.text: The wonder has the Unconscious condition until another creature winds it with the wonder's unique key for 1 minute. Once wound, the wonder operates for 10 days or until a creature touches the wonder with its key as a Utilize action to deactivate it, after which the wonder has the Unconscious condition until it is wound again.

action.name: Chime (Bonus Action)
action.text: The wonder chirps a merry, metronomic tune. The wonder chooses one ally that it can see within 60 feet. Until the start of the wonder's next turn, the target has Advantage on the next ability check it makes with a Musical Instrument or Tinker's Tools.

action.name: Sprint (Bonus Action)
action.text: The wonder takes the Dash action.

An activated flying wonder uses the Flying Wonder stat block. The wonder is an ally to you and your allies. monster.name: Gyrocopter Wonder [5.5e]

trait.name: Wind-Up Operation
trait.text: The wonder has the Unconscious condition until another creature winds it with the wonder's unique key for 1 minute. Once wound, the wonder operates for 10 days or until a creature touches the wonder with its key as a Utilize action to deactivate it, after which the wonder has the Unconscious condition until it is wound again.

monster.description:
A Mechanical Wonder is a semi-autonomous object imbued with magical power. Mechanical Wonders vary greatly in size and form depending on their function. A Mechanical Wonder is a dormant object until activated. To activate a Mechanical Wonder, you must wind the wonder with a handheld key unique to that wonder. It takes 1 minute to wind a Mechanical Wonder. While you wind it, you must take the Utilize action each turn. Once wound, a Mechanical Wonder remains activated for the duration specified in the wonder's description below.
This wagon-sized vehicle is made of brassy metal and has a spiral-shaped propeller atop it. Its midsection is open on two sides. Once wound, the gyrocopter wonder remains active for 8 hours. While active, the gyrocopter can be used as a vehicle; it requires one pilot. The gyrocopter wonder is a Huge object that weighs 500 pounds and has the following statistics: AC 14, HP 50, Speed 5 ft., and Fly Speed 20 ft. The gyrocopter can bear up to 2,000 pounds of cargo; if it bears any more than this, it deactivates. Eight spectral cords are mounted to the inside of the cargo bay. A creature riding in the gyrocopter wonder can take a Utilize action to attach itself to or detach itself from one of these cords. A creature attached to a cord can leap from the gyrocopter wonder and glide, moving up to 5 feet horizontally for every 1 foot it descends in the air. If a creature attached to a cord is ever more than 500 feet away from the gyrocopter, the cord immediately disappears and returns to the wonder.
Source: Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn p. 246

monster.name: Aranea [5.5e]
monster.speed: Walk 30 ft., Climb 30 ft. (spider or hybrid form only)

trait.name: Gear
trait.text: Sling.

trait.name: Spider Climb (Hybrid or Spider Form Only)
trait.text: The aranea can climb difficult surfaces, including along ceilings, without needing to make an ability check.

trait.name: Web Walker
trait.text: The aranea ignores movement restrictions caused by webs, and it knows the location of any other creature in contact with the same web.

action.name: Multiattack
action.text: The aranea makes two attacks, using Bite, Slam, or Sling in any combination.

action.name: Bite (Hybrid or Spider Form Only)
action.text: Melee Attack Roll: +5, reach 5 ft. Hit: 6 (1d6+3) Piercing damage plus 2 (1d4) Poison damage.

action.name: Slam
action.text: Melee Attack Roll: +5, reach 5 ft. Hit: 7 (1d8+3) Bludgeoning damage.

action.name: Sling (Humanoid or Hybrid Form Only)
action.text: Ranged Attack Roll: +5, range 30/120 ft. Hit: 8 (2d4+3) Bludgeoning damage.

action.name: Spellcasting
action.text:
The aranea casts one of the following spells, requiring no Material components and using Charisma as the spellcasting ability (spell save DC 12):
• At will: Friends, Silent Image • 1/day: Hold Person

action.name: Shape-Shift (Bonus Action)
action.text: The aranea shape-shifts into a humanoid form, into a humanoid-spider hybrid form, or back into its true spider form. Its game statistics are the same in each form, except where noted. Any equipment it is wearing or carrying isn't transformed.

monster.spells: Friends, Silent Image, Hold Person
monster.description:
Secretive Crafter and Trader Treasure: Individual
Araneas are reclusive shape-shifters. An aranea's natural form resembles a bulky, humpbacked spider with two short arms beneath its head. An aranea can shape-shift into a humanoid form or into a multiarmed humanoid-spider hybrid. Araneas live in insular communities, such as the Spider Swamp in Calimshan, where they create beautiful objects that express their artistry and which are sometimes traded to other communities. Most araneas prefer to avoid combat, befuddling their foes long enough to skitter to safety. Roll or choose a result from the Aranea Crafts table as inspiration for an aranea's crafting talent.
Aranea Crafts: 1d6 | The Aranea Is Skilled at Crafting... 1 | Exceptionally comfortable bedding. 2 | Furniture made of wood and canvas. 3 | Poisons that are soporific rather than lethal. 4 | Poultices and unguents from medicinal herbs. 5 | Silks with intricate web patterns. 6 | Stories with cleverly concealed morals.
The araneas (sometimes called "werespiders"; pl: araneas or: aranea) are a magical race of sentient, shape-changing spider-like creatures inhabiting the Spider Swamp in Calimshan.
Description: While they are not true lycanthropes, aranea can transform between the appearance of a humanoid and a giant monstrous spider. Their humanoid form is that of a Calishite human, a Calishite half-elf, or, in some rare cases, a drow. The form and gender they can take is fixed at birth. In their natural form, these creatures appear to be giant humpbacked spiders with some subtle differences. In this form they also have a pair of short arms ending in many-jointed fingers and double-jointed thumbs, which extend from below their mandibles. Oddly, their brain is not located in their head segment but in a large hump on their back. Aranea also can take on a third, hybrid form. This form is humanoid, but the aranea bears sharp fangs, has spinnerets in his or her hands, and has four eyes instead of two. On occasion, the hybrid form also includes additional arms, but never more than eight in total.
Abilities: An aranea in spider-like form. Aranea are inherently magical beings and can cast a certain number of spells much like a sorcerer or dragon can. They prefer illusion, enchantment, and charm spells and avoid ever casting fire spells. In hybrid or natural forms, aranea have poisonous bites and can throw webs.
Combat: Aranea try to avoid combat, but if pressed into it, they take advantage of their webs and spells, immobilizing or distracting the most powerful opponents first. They take prisoners and exchange them for ransom rather than killing them.
Trade: The aranea, in the disguise of human forms, trade silk, herbs, and poisons with nearby settlements, such as Almraiven and Volothamp. In 1370 DR, a group of them worked secretly for the Silverstars Trading Coster of Saradush.
Society: Aranea usually live alone within temperate forests or in small colonies of three to six individuals.
History: According to legend, the aranea were created by Calishite wizards during the Night Wars to infiltrate the ranks of the drow armies. When the wars ended, the "werespiders" were hunted down and killed or driven into the Spider Swamp. They became a neutral, pacifistic people. Originally, they were only able to change into drow, but after a while, some gained the ability to change into Calishite human or half-elf forms and returned to the human cities incognito as well as spreading out from Calimshan into the wider world. This allowed them to trade their silks, herbs, and poisons with the coastal city of Volothamp. For a brief time during the Eye Tyrant Wars of the Fifth Age of Calimshan, the aranea ceased their pacifism and joined in the fight against the beholder armies from the Alimir Mountains who were seeking to take over the entire Forest of Mir. The aranea only allied with the Calishite forces long enough to repel the eye tyrants, before the two "allies" turned on each other. Over 800 years after their banishment, in 290 DR, Qysara Shoon V blamed them for a plague that was ravaging Almraiven. As a result, they were nearly wiped out by Volothamp's military. During this time, some adopted the worship of Zanassu, a demon lord of spiders, for protection and came to inhabit a city that was once called Ajhuutal somewhere in the swamp. The Qysara banished their god back to the Abyss two years later, which led to a gradual degradation of their society while the priests of Zanassu desperately awaited their god's return for the next 1000 years. Unbeknownst to them, Selvetarm had defeated Zanassu and stolen his divine essence, though the aranea remained relatively peaceful.
Rumors & Legends: Some drow believe that araneas were transformed from drow for failing Lolth, the Spider Queen. Others maintain that araneas were Lolth's first creation before she perfected the drow.
Source: Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn p. 250

monster.name: Beast of Malar [5.5e]
monster.speed: Walk 50 ft., Burrow 40 ft. (land form only), Fly 60 ft. (sky form only), Swim 40 ft. (sea form only)

trait.name: Amphibious (Sea Form Only)
trait.text: The beast breathes air and water.

trait.name: Divine Immortality
trait.text: If the beast dies, its body dissolves into black goo, and it gains a new body after 1d10 days, reviving with all its Hit Points in a place of Malar's choosing.

trait.name: Legendary Resistance (3/Day)
trait.text: If the beast fails a saving throw, it can choose to succeed instead.

trait.name: Magic Resistance
trait.text: The beast has Advantage on saving throws against spells and other magical effects.

trait.name: Regeneration
trait.text: The beast regains 20 Hit Points at the start of its turn. If the beast takes Radiant damage or damage from a Critical Hit, this trait doesn't function at the start of the beast's next turn. The beast dies only if it starts its turn with 0 Hit Points and doesn't regenerate.

action.name: Multiattack
action.text: The beast makes three attacks, using Bite or Claws in any combination.

action.name: Bite
action.text: Melee Attack Roll: +9, reach 5 ft. Hit: 23 (4d8+5) Piercing damage.

action.name: Claws (Land or Sky Form Only)
action.text: Melee Attack Roll: +9, reach 5 ft. Hit: 18 (3d8+5) Slashing damage and if the target is Large or smaller, it has the Prone condition.

action.name: Recuperative Shape-Shift (Bonus Action)
action.text: The beast shape-shifts into its land form, sea form, or sky form and regains 9 (2d8) Hit Points. Its game statistics are the same in each form, except where noted. Any equipment it is wearing or carrying isn't transformed.

monster.description:
A Beast of Malar is a savage shape-changing creature, sacred to the god of the hunt Malar, whose only purpose in life is hunt, pursuit, and slaying of the prey.
Description: Ferocious, Shape-Changing Predator
Malar, god of the bestial hunt, sometimes manifests a spark of primal predation in physical form: the beast of Malar. The beast of Malar can take three types of forms—a land form, a sea form, and a sky form-to pursue prey across land, seas, and skies. In each form, its short fur is glossy black with red fur around its jaws and claws as though stained by the blood it has spilled. The beast of Malar has a muscular and unnatural appearance no matter its form; whether it resembles a bat, wolverine, or shark, there's no mistaking the beast of Malar for a mundane animal. The beast shifts easily between its forms to pursue its prey, using whichever shape suits it best to catch and kill its quarry. Normally only one beast of Malar exists at a time. However, Malar might create multiple beasts to pursue legendary prey or simply display his extraordinary ferocity.
Beasts of Malar can shift between three forms at will. The Hunting Panther form that resembles a panther of the Prime Material Plane with sinister glowing red eyes, Claw Slayer form that is similar to a wolverine, and the Bat form. All the creature's forms have black sheeny fur with red marking that looks like blood splatter on its face, paws, and shoulders.
Abilities: Beasts of Malar's shapeshifting ability also grants them powerful regenerative ability upon the shape change. This regeneration ability can heal even the wounds that are severe or uncurable by the regular regeneration. But the Beasts' killer instinct often stops them from taking advantage of the life-saving regeneration, as they fight to the death. The Beasts' regular regeneration is vulnerable to divine magic and blessed weapons.
Behavior: The Beasts' only purpose in life is the hunt, and they use the three forms' abilities to track and kill their opponents with terrifying effectiveness. The smooth and agile Hunting Panther form is perfect for tracking the unfortunate prey with its sharp senses and speed. The Claw Slayer form has scimitar-shaped front claws and sharp rear claws with elbow hooks that are perfect for quick climbing in pursuit. The Bat form is not the best flier but still is more than capable of tracking and pursuing the prey in the air. Unlike true bats, the Beasts of Malar do not possess echolocation and prefer to keep to the other more deadly forms.
Combat: The Hunting Panther form likes to toy with its prey like many other cats of the Prime Material plane. When faced with multiple adversaries, the Beast in the Panther form dashes past front-line defenders to rend and gore spellcasters. The Panther's pounce can knock the prey down which opens the Beast to its fearsome raking attacks with the front paws.
The Claw Slayer's strategy is grabbing the prey with its sharp teeth and goring the opponent with all four appendages' claws.
The Bat form is not good for combat, but great for scouting.
Ecology: The beast of Malar is not a true animal, so it does not have any other purpose but to hunt and kill. Upon its death, the beast is returned to the Malar's realm only to be rewarded and reincarnated if the deity is satisfied with the creature's hunt.
History: The worshipers of Malar, especially the northern barbarian tribes, evil rangers, dark druids, and the People of the Black Blood celebrated Shieldmeet by commencing a unicorn hunt using the Beasts of Malar. During the rest of the year, the People of the Black Blood hunted the adventurers for sport with the Beasts.
In 1372 DR, they could occasionally be found within the Forest of Lethyr.
Notable Beasts of Malar • Burak, an infamous half-orcish pirate of the Moonsea in the late 14th century DR had a loyal companion beast of Malar on board of the Flotsam. • Methim was the companion of Alaffinel, a disgraced half-celestial that was on the run from his kin across the planes circa 1370 DR.
Source: Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn p. 251

monster.name: Cultist of Bane [5.5e]

trait.name: Gear
trait.text: Breastplate, Holy Symbol.

trait.name: Determined Survivor
trait.text: The cultist regains 10 Hit Points at the start of each of its turns if it is Bloodied and has at least 1 Hit Point.

action.name: Multiattack
action.text: The cultist makes three attacks, using Gauntlet or Oppressive Burst in any combination. It can replace one attack with a use of Spellcasting to cast Dominate Person, if available.

action.name: Gauntlet
action.text: Melee Attack Roll: +8, reach 5 ft. Hit: 17 (3d8+4) Bludgeoning damage.

action.name: Oppressive Burst
action.text: Ranged Attack Roll: +8, range 120 ft. Hit: 16 (2d10+5) Psychic damage and the target can't take Reactions until the start of the cultist's next turn.

action.name: Spellcasting
action.text:
Spellcasting. The cultist casts one of the following spells, using Wisdom as the spellcasting ability (spell save DC 16):
• 1/day: Dominate Person • 2/day each: Calm Emotions, Detect Thoughts

reaction.name: Counterattack
reaction.text: Trigger: The cultist is hit by an attack roll. Response: The cultist makes one Gauntlet or Oppressive Burst attack against the triggering creature.

monster.spells: Dominate Person, Calm Emotions, Detect Thoughts
monster.description:
Wicked Zealots of the Dead Three Treasure: Individual, Relics
The adventurers Bane, Bhaal, and Myrkul seized divinity but were slain for their hubris. All three have been reborn and are now known as the Dead Three. Each of the Dead Three has inspired wicked cults that follow their paths of tyranny, murder, and necromancy. More than any other gods, the Dead Three directly influence Faerün-and particularly the city of Baldur's Gate —in malign ways. Cultists who receive orders from their patron god directly are often the most ambitious and most dangerous.
Cultist of Bane: Cultists of Bane sow strife, either by directly bullying others or by abusing existing power structures to create division and oppression. Although many cultists of Bane are tyrants capable of influencing large groups of lackeys, other cultists prefer to operate from the shadows. These cultists use their forceful personalities to counsel well-intentioned rulers, turning benign organizations into dictatorships and twisting leaders into tyrants. They tattoo Bane's symbol on their hands as a sign of devotion.
Cultists of Bane, the Faerûn's god of tyranny, strife, and control, seek to reshape the world through absolute order and fear. They operate in highly organized, martial hierarchies, viewing themselves not as mindless destroyers, but as lawful conquerors whose ultimate duty is to control and rule the weak.
Church of Bane: The Church of Bane is the organization dedicated to worshiping, as well as furthering the influence of the deity, Bane. Generally speaking, they are a cruel and power-hungry group of individuals who worship their deity under a strict hierarchy.
Beliefs: The church of Bane believes in subservience and submission within their hierarchy, with junior members bowing, kneeling, or even kissing the feet of their superior, depending on their rank. Superior members are to be followed and obeyed at all times. The rules in the church are of the utmost importance, but those from any other lands or faith are entirely meaningless. Bane's authority and divinity are revered above all else. According to his priests, Bane is to be feared by his faithful and even more feared by the unfaithful. It is the duty of every member of the church of Bane to "spread (his) fear".
Attitude: Banite priests take great pride in their ability to control their actions and avoid succumbing to emotional outbursts. Their outward demeanor is cold and thoughtful, they think carefully before they speak, often preferring sarcasm and "witty banter" rather than overt hostility.
Activities: The overarching goal of Bane's clergy is the charge of seizing or manipulating their way into power in every nation, city-state or freehold in all of Faerûn, to bring them under his influence. Using emotionally manipulative tools such as fear, hatred or greed to sow conflict, war and chaos allows the Black Hand to maintain control over lands too distressed to maintain stability. To this end, priests and followers are encouraged to commit acts such as torture, political infiltration or inciting mayhem with subtlety, cruelty and overall, fear.
Titles: • High Imperceptor: Serving as the apex in the hierarchy of Bane's church, this leader is the supreme servant of the Black Lord. • Deep Mystery: A general rank for the higher-tier clergy members including (in descending order) High Inquisitor, Grand Bloodletter, Dark Imperceptor, Imperceptor, Lord/Lady of the Hand, Lord/Lady of Mysteries and Vigilator. • Dreadmaster: A title granted to certain priests of Bane that mostly keep low-level positions within the church.
Knightly orders: • Knights of the Black Gauntlet: An order of black knights and helmed horrors from the city of Mintar led by Lord Knight Imperceptor Teldorn Darkhope.
Monastic Orders: • Order of the Iron Gauntlet: A small sect of Bane worshipping monks within the Zhentarim, specially trained in stealth and assassination. In 1372 DR, they were led by the Half-elf Mara Kalaliv, who had been commanded by Scyllua Darkhope to recruit and train up the monastic order.
Rituals: Rituals of Bane are to be performed whenever ordered by senior clergy members and hold no correlation to any seasonal shifts, marks on the calendar or specific holy days. They are held either outdoors at night, or in a space of darkness, such as darkened chambers, caves or ruins with only dim lighting. A Black Altar is prepared; consisting of a plain stone block which, if obsidian is unavailable, is painted black or draped in black fabric. To accompany the altar is either a floating, stone Hand of Bane or, failing that, an empty black throne facing its direction. Services include rhythmic chanting, the rolling beating of drums and the sacrifice of an intelligent creature's life. To prepare for this life to be given to Bane, the oblatory life is to be demeaned and tortured until they show him due fear.
Temples: • The Obsidian Chapel: the temple to Bane that stood in Anauroch and housed the enchanted Loviatan weapon - the Icon of Power. The temple was plundered by Bedine raiders sometime long before 1281 DR. • A temple of Bane could be found in Undermountain. The sect that maintained that temple still worshiped Bane following his demise during the Time of Troubles. By mid 14th century DR, the leadership of the temple was taken over by wizards as they still had access to spells, unlike loyal baneites. Eventually, the Undermountain temple was abandoned by living followers of Bane, leaving only baneguard to defend it from scavengers and adventurers. • The Black Lord's Altar in Mulmaster, considered for a time to be the centre of power for the High Imperceptor and Banite church. • The Black Altar in Zhentil Keep, the result of a splinter in the church instigated by Fzoul Chembryl. It was destroyed a number of times, contested, and at different stages was reconsecrated to both Cyric and Iyachtu Xvim. • The House of the Black Lord in the Ruins of Zhentil Keep, originally dedicated to the tyrant god's progeny, Iyachtu Xvim. • The largest temple of Bane in the time between his death, and subsequent return, was the Black Lord's Cloak in the city of Mourktar in the land of Threskel. It was led by the self-appointed Dread Imperceptor Kabbarath Telthaug, who separated himself and his clergy from the greater church of Bane some time before the Time of Troubles. The temple was served by over 700 ranked Banite priests, posessed a clergy of over 1000 and even had a loyal and disciplined army, who had enjoyed numerous victories in Chessenta.
Equipment: Clergy of the church of Bane dress in black and are sure to always remain armed. For ceremonial purposes, the priests adorn black armor draped in blood-red capes while mages don ceremonial black robes that have been affixed with illusion spells to present shimmering black stars or blood spilling out. The prestige and rank of the individual Banite is evident by the craftsmanship of their armor or robes. When on a mission outside their temples, the priests keep in their armor and mages wear more appropriate, although similarly themed, traveling robes. No member of the church adorns vestments that would hamper their attempts of subterfuge or infiltration, if it is so needed in their service of Bane. Unfortunately, the popularity of facial tattoos among Bane's faithful often makes them stand out regardless of what they wore. Many Banites bear baneswords, enchanted longswords that are forged in great number for the Black Lord's clergy.
History: The church of Bane began its entrenchment in Zhentil Keep, or what was then-called Flostren's Hold, in the mid-8th century DR. Long before the beginning of the Era of Upheaval, due in part to the ambitions of one Fzoul Chembryl, there was a great schism within the church of Bane. A fierce rivalry emerged between the orthodox and Transformed sects of his worship.
Splintering: After Bane's death during the Time of Troubles, his church underwent significant changes and the rift between his warring sects intensified. Even more troubling, The Mad God Cyric assumed his portfolio, granted spells to his priests and attempted to convert them to his direct worship. The Orthodox members of the faith saw Cyric as Bane's new form and, along with former faithful of Bhaal and Myrkul, were adamant followers of the Prince of Lies. The group of Banites that followed the Transformation saw Bane as truly dead, insisting that Cyric assumed his portfolio of strife. They maintained a reverence of that office of power and Cyric as its holder. Some more smaller sects of Bane-worship emerged in this time such as the ultra-orthodox Risen Cult of Bane in the Moonshae Isles. They maintained that Bane was still alive following the Avatar Crisis and that Cyric, whom they referred to as "the Pretender", usurped his power and would face a divine punishment upon Bane's return. By 1361 DR almost all of Bane's clergy had converted to the worship of Cyric, with few holdouts in the Moonsea and more specifically Zhentil Keep. By this time Cyric had grown impatient and frustrated and his followers carried out an inquest against the remaining Banites in Zhentil Keep that would come to be known as the Banedeath. Over the period of a tenday, all remaining temples, shrines or other evidence of Bane's worship were purged from the city. The last remnants of the true church of Bane went underground while a small group began reverence to Iyachtu Xvim, Bane's divine son. The High Imperceptor of Bane went in hiding during these years.
Source: Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn p. 254

action.text:
Spellcasting. The cultist casts one of the following spells, using Wisdom as the spellcasting ability (spell save DC 14):
• 1/day each: Dimension Door, Mislead • 2/day: Mind Spike

monster.description:
Wicked Zealots of the Dead Three Treasure: Individual, Relics
The adventurers Bane, Bhaal, and Myrkul seized divinity but were slain for their hubris. All three have been reborn and are now known as the Dead Three. Each of the Dead Three has inspired wicked cults that follow their paths of tyranny, murder, and necromancy. More than any other gods, the Dead Three directly influence Faerün-and particularly the city of Baldur's Gate —in malign ways. Cultists who receive orders from their patron god directly are often the most ambitious and most dangerous.
Cultist of Bhaal: Cultists of Bhaal revel in bloodshed. They enjoy the act of murder, particularly when they can use inventive methods that instill fear among witnesses. Cultists of Bhaal sometimes form cabals of assassins or mercenaries, but they perform their brutal slaughter for the perverse love of bloodshed and honor to their sinister god rather than for financial recompense. These cunning serial killers and mass murderers remain a step ahead of investigators, at least until the cultists' zealous bloodlust overwhelms their senses.
The Cult of Bhaal consists of ruthless, terror-driven zealots who worship the Faerûnian god of murder Bhaal. They operate in shadowy, scattered networks, carrying out ritualistic killings to spread fear and resurrect or empower their lord.
Church of Bhaal: The Church of Bhaal is the religious organization that is devoted to the worship of the Lord of Murder, Bhaal.
Organization: The clergy of the Lord of Murder are a disorganised group of evil priests and assassins. Priests of Bhaal are referred to as either Bhaalists, which is most common to the west of the Dragon Reach, or Bhaalyn, which is used to the east. In cities and towns, members of the Church of Bhaal are often clerics, whilst in far removed locations, they are usually deathstalkers.
• High Primate/Primistress: Members of a specific faction (or an area) of the Church of Bhaal are always led by a High Primate or High Primistress. • Primate/Primistress: A Primate or Primistress is in charge of a specific fortress or temple, which are filled with assassins an agents. • First Murder: First Murders are assistants to Primates and Primistresses, and help with sending agents to nearby settlements. In other faiths, such a role is known as a scion. • Cowled Death: Cowled Deaths, who occupy offices in the community, make up the senior clergy of the Church of Bhaal. Nine Cowled Deaths report to each First Murder. • Deathdealer: Deathdealers form the more common members of the Church of Bhaal, and are underneath the Cowled Deaths. They bear the title of Slaying Hand.
Activities: As expected, Bhaalists' main activities consist of preparing for and carrying out assassinations, hunting bounties, and straight up bloody murder. Such preparations include sourcing and maintaining weapons and other gear, training, journeying, and praying. Bhaalists generally put a lot of time into researching who to murder, as well as the location and time to commit it. High priority targets often include rivals, as well as victims who would be missed by the common folk; this helps to rake in donations and other types of offerings. Bhaal does not just urge his clergy to carry out killings, but also to seek the wealth that comes along with it.
Rituals: Aside from holy killings, Bhaalists observe several rituals. Many are done privately, such as when a priest is planned to ascend to a high rank. In this instance, the member of the church heads out and performs a killing with only their bare hands. After completion, they secretly inform a higher member of the church. The senior member then organizes a public ceremony, where all members don their ceremonial outfits, and an honorary killing to Bhaal is made.
• Day's Farewell: A formal ritual that is taken part of by the entire clergy when the day draws to a close, as well as when a member sets off for duty. • Feast of the Moon: This ritual is the only one of its type that is set to occur on a specific date. During the ritual feast, priests of Bhaal praise and discuss particularly unique or interesting kills, as well as remember those who have died in service to the Lord of Murder. One of the most retold stories is that of Uthaedeol's legendary murder of King Samyte of Tethyr.
Base of Operations: Urban members of the Church of Bhaal congregate in underground temples. Such temples are sometimes decorated in the theme of murder and death, from sculptures of a vicious murder, to mosaics. Many of these sites have rooms filled with multiple corpses (as well as tokens from the deceased), if the bodies cannot be left at the site of the killing. Rural members instead prefer to worship the Lord of Murder at ancient shrines and oblational altars. Such shrines are usually built atop infrequently-visited tops of hills, and are shaped in the symbol of Bhaal. The most well-known base is the Tower of Swift Death in Thay. Others exist around the continent, such as the Temple of Bhaal in the Undercity of Baldur's Gate, the Stronghold in Delimbiyr Vale (which formerly acted as a Bhaalist monastery), and the Temple of Bhaal in the Forest of Wyrms.
Vestments: All Bhaalists, during ceremonies and other temple work, wear a combination of purple or black cowls and robes. Such garments are often streaked in violet, in a seemingly random combination. Every other part of their outfit is black, including the interior and veil. Senior priests are known to add additions to their outfits, such as a red sash, so they are identifiable during rituals in dim settings. Curved ceremonial daggers are utilized by all members of the church, though only the highest members of the clergy (as well as Brethren of the Keen Strike) directly use them in their murderous acts.
Dogma: Bhaalists see murder as not just a duty, but as pleasure. When they commit murder, they make sure their victims know that it is the Lord of Murder behind the killing. Each member strongly believes that every single murder they commit strengthens their master. They are required to kill once every tenday during the darkest time of the night. This is not always possible, as a Bhaalist could be incarcerated; once released, they have to make up for their killings twice over. Make all folk fear Bhaal. Let your killings be especially elegant, or grisly, or seem easy so that those observing them are awed or terrified. Tell folk that gold proffered to the church can make the Lord of Murder overlook them for today. — Bhaalist dogma
Orders: The Church of Bhaal supports many organizations that perform duties on behalf of the Lord of Murder.
• Brethren of the Keen: Strike The Brethren of the Keen Strike are a society of which all speciality priests of Bhaal are included in. • Shadow Thieves of Amn: The Shadow Thieves are a deadly group of rogues, money-lenders, and assassins based in Crimmor, Amn. • Citadel of Assassins: The Assassins Guild of the Galenas is an organization of highly trained killers that is led by the Grandfather of Assassins.
Ancient History: Long before the 14th century DR, Bhaal ascended to godhood in a strange bargain with Jergal; after this his church came to form. His church would expand over Faerûn, but two generic factions would form: those who dwelt in urban areas, and those who dwelt in rural areas. The relations between those two sets of worshipers was fairly neutral, as well as distant.
14th century DR: In 1358 DR, Bhaal was forced to walk the ground of Faerûn as a mortal. On Eleasis 13 of that year, Bane and Myrkul were determined to increase the power of the Lord of Darkness. The mastermind, Myrkul, came up with a plan to produce an enormous death spell, which would kill all true assassins of the Realms. In turn, their life-force would be absorbed by Bane in a ritual known as the Stealing of the Souls. As the plan was executed, a large amount of Bhaal's agents and worshipers perished immediately. Later on that year, Bhaal was murdered by Cyric the Dark Sun, and many of his temples and clergy were converted to Cyricism. During this time, his church referred to their new master as Cyric-Bhaal. After 1361 DR, the Dark Sun would impose order among the converted members of the Church of Bhaal, and many eventually came to worship Cyric as their true lord. However, the rural faction would retain their belief in the Lord of Murder, as they were still granted spells in his name. The differences between the rural and urban factions would became great, and in 1367 DR, they were known to have ambushed each other. As of that time, the rural worshipers of Bhaal stopped receiving spells in their master's name. As such, many converted to the Church of Cyric, or even the Church of Iyachtu Xvim. However, not all turned to the worship to members of the Faerûnian pantheon, and instead venerated deities of the Orc pantheon, as well as other non-human groups of divine beings. Still, some did not turn from the Lord of Murder; ancient priests would lead their clergy in remote places scattered around the continent. Though the worship of Bhaal mostly faded away, Bhaal planned to return. He had in fact foreseen his death, and scattered his essence in his mortal progeny, the Bhaalspawn.
15th century DR: In 1482 DR, the two final Bhaalspawn, Abdel Adrian and Viekang, engaged in a fight. The victor was transformed into the Slayer, Bhaal was reborn, and his church began to operate once more. As of the Second Sundering, Bhaal remained behind in mortal form as a quasi-deity, and his church became known as a "cult". Together with Myrkulytes and Banites, Bhaalists began to terrorize the Realms once more, particularly in Baldur's Gate. Reports claimed that the Lord of Murder was known to make visits to a secretive temple of this city in person.
Source: Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn p. 255

monster.name: Cultist of Myrkul [5.5e]

trait.name: Gear

action.name: Necrotic Burst

monster.spells: Speak with Dead, Thaumaturgy, Animate Dead, Circle of Death
monster.description:
Wicked Zealots of the Dead Three Treasure: Individual, Relics
The adventurers Bane, Bhaal, and Myrkul seized divinity but were slain for their hubris. All three have been reborn and are now known as the Dead Three. Each of the Dead Three has inspired wicked cults that follow their paths of tyranny, murder, and necromancy. More than any other gods, the Dead Three directly influence Faerün-and particularly the city of Baldur's Gate —in malign ways. Cultists who receive orders from their patron god directly are often the most ambitious and most dangerous.
Cultist of Myrkul: Cultists of Myrkul dominate the dead, whether to raise Undead servants, terrorize the living, or extract secrets known only to the deceased. Most are more interested in amassing knowledge than power or wealth. Many cultists of Myrkul are sinister manipulators who hoard necromantic lore and gather in cults to share their gruesome secrets. Such secrets often require unsavory experimentation, which these heartless cultists relish.
Cultists of Myrkul worship the Lord of Bones, a god of death, decay, and the inevitable end of all things. Their core lore revolves around hoarding necromantic secrets, harvesting body parts for dark rituals, and manipulating the dead to terrify the living
Church of Myrkul: The church of Myrkul, also known as the Gray Ones, or (disparagingly) Fingerbones, is the predominant organization dedicated to the worship and veneration of the Lord of the Dead, Myrkul. It is not a popular faith in Faerûn, whose members are often looked upon as secretive, morbid loners, who are obsessed with death and enjoy seeing fear in others. While that might be the case in some instances, they are dedicated to the care of the dying and deceased. Myrkulytes view death with profound respect and take great care to help those who are dying feel as comfortable as possible, tending to their last wishes, presiding over funerals, and serving as undertakers and caretakers in cemeteries across the Realms.
Beliefs: They believe that death is an inevitability of life, an aspect that mortals should not attempt to flee. As such, they hold the influence of the dead in extremely high regard.
Attitudes: While many Faerûnians openly make offerings to Myrkul out of fear, such as during funeral services or when honoring their dead, his clergy are more secretive in their worship. As is the common perception, these faithful are a reclusive and macabre lot who remain stoic, almost aloof, to their surroundings. They often conceal their pre-church lives from their fellow clergy and membership within the church from those outside. Yet there are some followers of Myrkul that sincerely romanticize the concept of death and join due to their attraction to the teachings of Myrkul's high priests.
Activities: The Myrkulyte clergy are tasked with making the mortals of Faerûn fear and respect death, as well as the power of Myrkul. They are expected to propagate two seemingly conflicting beliefs about themselves. First, that their clergy possess absolute patience and trustworthiness, and second, that touching them would bring upon certain death. Their actions are meant to reflect these "truths". They share stories of the church's doombringers, champions of Myrkul who travel Faerûn avenging the deaths of those to whom they have sword oaths or slaying those who mock the Lord of Bones.
A cleric of Myrkul.: In service to others, Myrkulyte clerics travel the Realms offering burial and funeral services to the loved ones of the recently-deceased, for a fee. When called upon to assist the dying, they do all in their power to make them comfortable, offering their perspective that death is a inevitable transition from life. Whenever it is required they assist those who are dying with their remaining affairs, such as final decrees and last wills and testaments. In return for a "skull fee" a Myrkulyte priest acts as an agent for someone after their death, carrying out any final arrangements or deeds they could not complete in life.
Studies: Priests of Myrkul are experienced necrologists, in that they spend much of their time studying lore regarding the undead. They are well-versed in their identification abilities.
Organization: There are few clerics of Myrkul found in Faerûn, compared to other faiths. They refer to one another as "Death" or, for senior members, "Most Holy Death".
Titles: The titles within the church of Myrkul are tied to specific rituals and duties they perform upon ascension to that rank. In descending order they are:
• Elder Doom > Deathbringer > Withering Lord > Undead Master > Ritual Consecrator > Bone Dancer > Crypt Carver > Shroud Wearer > Bone Talker > Night Walker > Daring One
Orders: • Knights of the Undying Dragon: This long-forgotten order of death knights have served as the champions of Myrkul for decades.
Rituals: Prayers to Myrkul are offered at dusk, while his faithful are expected to perform their personal worship during in the darkness of night. Myrkulyte priests are rarely allowed to raise the dead on their own accord. However they perform the rite for those of other faiths who bring a dead body to one of their temples.
• The dusking is a ritual performed as a reminder of the world's collective mortality, that death is waiting for every living being on Toril. The non-faithful are allowed to make offerings to appease the Lord of the Dead. • The bone dance, lead by the faith's Bone Dancers, is performed to summon undead guardians to protect an item or location of significance to the church.
Holy Days: The church of Myrkul observes one day of remembrance that is linked to the calendar of Harptos. The Day the Dead are Most With Us, which lands between the months of Uktar and Nightal, is seen as the time of the year where the spirits of the dead rise from the Underworld and float unseen across Toril. It is believed they seek out their surviving loved ones and descendants, and leave silent messages to them throughout the day. Mykulytes celebrate the dead with chants and hymns, culminating in the Flagons of the Fallen ritual which is performed at midnight.
Bases: Temples of Myrkul are an uncommon sight in Faerûn, typically taking the form of a mausoleum built above sprawling, subterranean necropolis. Their exteriors are often adorned with gargoyles and shrouded by the smoke of their crematories. Within their underground halls are scores of stone statues of dead and decaying men, women and children. There are scores of undead roaming the chambers of these crypts, the most prominent of which are skeletal in nature.
Temples: • Legacy of Deep Death: The only temple of Myrkul that was established after the Time of Troubles was established by three Myrkulyte liches on the sea bed under the Sea of Swords. • Skullspire: This massive spire in Tulmon was the meeting place of the Conclave of Doom, serving as the training area for initiates and staging area for activities performed by the lesser clerics. • Temple of Myrkul in Undermountain: The temple that held the holy artifact, the Black Wand of Myrkul. After Myrkul's death, the temple was mostly abandoned, with just a few loyal worshipers attending to the shrines inside. By 1370 DR, the temple was briefly torn between two factions trying to calm it. The followers of Kelemvor were trying to claim the temple as their deity inherited Myrkul's portfolio, and the Sardonyx Knights of Grumbar were attempting to convert it to their own religion.
Dress: Priests of Myrkul wear black, hooded robes, tied around the waist with a single white sash. While they always wear skull-shaped half-masks in public, they show their faces and walk barefoot when within their temples. Any exposed skin is concealed with ash. When venturing out in the Realms, they wear the finest armor underneath their hooded cloaks.
History: While Myrkul himself ascended to godhood from a mortal life eons ago, the divinity was first encountered by his future initiates when a speak with dead spell was cast upon the head priest of some ancient temple. The Lord of the Dead conveyed his dogma through the vessel of the body. After the death of Myrkul in the Time of Troubles, his divine domain was transferred by Ao to the newly-ascended Cyric, or "Cyruk" as he was known to Myrkulytes. The stoic and largely-emotionless priests were unfazed by this change, and they offered no organized resistance or any emotional reaction. A decade later when Cyric was defeated by Kelemvor in the City of Strife, the transition of worship from the Myrkulyte-Cyricists to the new god of the dead was just as smooth of a transition. While some remnant Myrkul's energy was transferred into the nearby artifact, the Crown of Horns, for all intents and purposes, the church of Myrkul was considered dead by the people of Faerûn. However, that which was dead could not truly die. After Myrkul's death, a temple in his name was constructed beneath the Sea of Swords, in the area where Midnight cast away the brown miasma that was released upon the destruction of the deity's avatar. After the Second Sundering Myrkul was restored as the Reaper, the god of death who brought the souls he had claimed to Kelemvor, the god of the dead. Kelemvor would then judge the fate of the souls. There were few actual temples of Myrkul in the late 15th century, but nearly every human cemetery or mausoleum was engraved with Myrkul's holy symbol.
Source: Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn p. 255

monster.name: Dead Three Scion [5.5e]

trait.name: Culling Aura
trait.text: Constitution Saving Throw: DC 20, each Bloodied creature in a 30-foot Emanation originating from the scion at the end of the scion's turn. Failure: The target can't regain Hit Points until the start of the scion's next turn.

trait.name: Legendary Resistance (3/Day)
trait.text: If the scion fails a saving throw, it can choose to succeed instead.

trait.name: Magic Resistance
trait.text: The scion has Advantage on saving throws against spells and other magical effects.

action.name: Multiattack
action.text: The scion makes two attacks, using Death Touch or Mindwrack Bolt in any combination.

action.name: Death Touch
action.text: Melee Attack Roll: +12, reach 5 ft. Hit: 25 (4d8+7) Necrotic damage.

action.name: Mindwrack Bolt
action.text: Ranged Attack Roll: +12, range 120 ft. Hit: 21 (6d6) Psychic damage and the target has the Poisoned condition until the start of the scion's next turn.

action.name: Spellcasting
action.text:
The scion casts one of the following spells, requiring no Material components and using Charisma as the spellcasting ability (spell save DC 20):
• At will: Detect Thoughts, Dispel Magic • 2/day each: Dimension Door, Invisibility, Scrying • 1/day each: Circle of Death, Create Undead

legendary.name: Legendary Actions (3/Turn)
legendary.text: Legendary Actions Uses: 3/Turn. Immediately after another creature's turn, the dead three scion can expend a use to take one of the following actions. The dead three scion regains all expended uses at the start of each of its turns.

legendary.name: Attack
legendary.text: The scion makes a Death Touch or Mindwrack Bolt attack.

legendary.name: Command
legendary.text: The scion casts Command (level 2 version), using the same spellcasting ability as Spellcasting. The scion can't take this action again until the start of its next turn.

monster.spells: Command, Detect Thoughts, Dispel Magic, Dimension Door, Invisibility, Scrying, Circle of Death, Create Undead
monster.description:
Inheritor of a Malevolent Deific Triumvirate Treasure: Relics
Some wicked mortals have bound their souls to Bane, Bhaal, and Myrkul and gained a portion of malevolent divine power from each. A scion of the Dead Three might have seized this power in a sinister ritual or had it thrust on them by an evil Artifact or a god's malevolent will. In any case, they possess cruelty, bloodlust, and necromantic power in equal measure and serve the Dead Three with their soul. A Dead Three scion leads cults to Bane, Bhaal, or Myrkul-and often to all three. Sometimes the scion commands a single cult with an uneasy mix of adherents of each god, but a scion might lead separate cults from the shadows, playing them against each other and coordinating their efforts to bring the greatest amount of misery to a region.
A Scion of the Three is an agent or cursed champion who draws macabre occult powers from the Dead Three—the malevolent trio of gods who were once power-hungry mortals from Baldur's Gate. This dark lineage manifests as bloodthirsty reflexes, teleportation abilities, and the capacity to strike terrifying fear into enemies. The lore surrounding these gods and their scions is rooted deeply in the history of Faerûn:
The Dark Ascension: Long before Dale Reckoning, Bane (the tyrant), Bhaal (the assassin), and Myrkul (the necromancer) made a pact to achieve godhood or die trying. They scoured the realms to steal the portfolio of Jergal, the Lord of the End of Everything. When Jergal willingly handed over his throne to them, they bickered over who would rule, deciding their domains by chance.
The Dead Three: They are known as the "Dead Three" because they were famously killed during the Time of Troubles, though they eventually returned. Bane governs tyranny and hatred, Bhaal oversees violence and murder, and Myrkul rules over the dead and decaying.
Scion Powers: Scions are most heavily concentrated in Baldur's Gate. Underground cults employ them as assassins and enforcers, though some scions are bound to their dark patron against their will via a curse. Mechanically, a scion can call upon these entities to gain specific resistances and spells. For example, they can channel Bane for psychic resistance, Bhaal for poison resistance, or Myrkul for necrotic resistance.
Source: Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn p. 256

monster.description:
Dragons of Caverns and Secrets Treasure: Arcana
Deep dragons slither through the wet and lightless places of the Underdark. They are stealthy hunters with an affinity for lost lore and fungi that flourish in the depths. As deep dragons age, their smooth, serpentine bodies become riddled with fungal rot, particularly around their faces, to imbue their breath with terror-inducing spores. Deep dragons covet treasure and knowledge. Some deep dragons seek to gain knowledge via experience and travel, slithering through caverns and seas of the Underdark to map hidden passages for dozens of miles. Other deep dragons enjoy cultivating groves of molds and fungi, including colossal varieties sufficient to conceal the dragons sinuous forms. Many deep dragons collect forgotten tomes or works of art and bully, cajole, or steal collections from drow or duergar sages. Deep dragons are excellent swimmers. They often clash with aquatic Underdark societies, such as kuotoa. Many deep dragons demand tribute from these groups in the form of food or treasure. Underdark explorers have many reasons to brave deep dragon lairs beyond treasure hunting; they might contain the only surviving copies of forgotten lore, fungal ingredients for cures or plagues, or maps to lost Underdark locales.
Deep Dragon Wyrmling: Deep dragon wyrmlings are lithe with a narrow frame and flexible wings. They slip through crevasses in the Underdark, from which they hunt to satisfy their voracious appetites.
Deep dragons, also called purple dragons, drakes of the depths, and silent hunters, are a type of chromatic dragon that lives in the Underdark.
Description: Despite their large size, deep dragons are slender and agile, and their snakelike bodies, narrow wings, and thin limbs allow them to crawl through the tunnels of the Underdark. Their scales are smooth, and in the light, an adult dragon's scales are the color of amethyst, while in the dark, they appear nearly black. In general, older specimens have much darker scales, while younger ones have more purple or maroon coloration. Older deep dragons are known to develop fungal growths around their heads and necks. A dragon egg can be identified as that of a deep dragon by the purple tinge seen when held in front of an intense white light, though it shares this trait with shadow dragon and amethyst dragon eggs.
Personality: Deep dragons are patient and cunning. They prioritize their own survival above all else, yet are known to relish the opportunity to hunt or even fight if the situation demands it. They prefer to manipulate and negotiate rather than to risk combat, and are crafty dealmakers. They are quick to disregard any creature that isn't useful to them. Deep dragons collect trivia, insights, tricks, and knowledge from far flung places, and delight in acquiring new information. They are known to collect magic items, not simply to hoard but also to use for themselves. Some deep dragons enjoy assuming the form of drow and infiltrating the dark elves' cities in disguise.
Abilities: In order to better allow them to navigate the narrow underground tunnels which they call home, deep dragons develop potent innate magical powers, including the ability to transmute rock to mud, and to cast spells like passwall, freedom of movement, and stone shape. Perhaps their most distinctive ability is their unique shapechanging power which develops as they age. The first form they learn to adopt is that of a winged snake, which does not reduce their overall size but allows them to slither and fly unimpeded by extra limbs. The second form they learn to adopt is that of a normal humanoid, and they can alter this form's appearance as with a polymorph self spell. Deep dragons are incapable of becoming intoxicated.
Combat: The claws of a deep dragon are intended to dig through solid rock, and as such, are devastating in combat even against heavily armored enemies. They prefer to pick off their enemies strategically, stalking them in the dark before pouncing or triggering a rockfall to bury them. A deep dragon's breath weapon attacks creatures' minds, and causes the target to be dazed or dominated, depending on the strength of the wyrm. These effects are attributed to fungal spores that the dragon exhales. They are also known to be able to breathe a cone of gas that is caustic to flesh. Deep dragons are harmed by direct sunlight.
Ecology: Purple dragons inhabit the Underdark, and are rarely known on the surface. However, younger specimens are known to occasionally venture upward, generally with some mission to claim a treasure or exact revenge on a foe, but sometimes just for the sake of exploration. Young deep dragons rarely leave the lairs of their parents until they have mastered both their serpentine and humanoid alternative forms. Lairs are located in the Upperdark and Middledark, usually no deeper than 7 miles (11 kilometers), and are highly idiosyncratic: some are built within ancient ruins, others on the shores of underground lakes, and others are carved out of masses of living fungus. Regardless, most of these lairs are full of secret passages to allow the dragon to make quick escapes and to prepare surprise ambushes. Lairs are often difficult to access, even for the dragon itself without using its serpentine or humanoid form, and are filled with traps and servants to protect the dragon's hoard, especially for times when the dragon ventures out to seek new information or treasures. They are known to transplant dangerous specimens of fungi into their lairs to serve as traps, and in general, underground varietals of fungi often abound around deep dragons' lairs and even on their bodies. Their magic, and this somewhat symbiotic relationship with underground fungus, is said to be a result of their species' exposure to the pervading magic of the Underdark.
Diet: Deep dragons prefer "seafood" including clams, fish, kuo-toa, and even aboleths. That said, they are known to eat nearly anything, and it is not uncommon for Underdark societies to trade with a deep dragon by offering them food in the form of humanoid prisoners.
Uses: The claw of a deep dragon can be used as a special component in the casting of the dragon blight spell. Their scales are also highly-prized by drow wizards, used in the formation of their everdark ink.
Society: Deep dragons value and hoard knowledge, and prefer to collect unique treasures with interesting backstories. They meticulously organize their hoards, even framing or displaying their favorite pieces, and they delight in giving long tours to guests, particularly other deep dragons. While some actively avoid revealing themselves to other types of dragons, most enjoy their company. Deep dragons tend to look down on "inferior" creatures, but can be encountered near drow cities working as guardians for the drow, expecting to be paid for their services with a steady supply of food in the form of captives and criminals. However, other drow cities are highly distrustful and fearful of deep dragons. The drow of Menzoberranzan actively hunt down any deep dragon they learn of, and this in turn leads a group of four nearby deep dragons to plot against the city. They regularly visit the city under shapeshifted disguise, noting the weaknesses of the drow and opportune prey among the visitors of the city Bazaar. They are not above working with non-dragons, but treat them either as servants or subordinates. They are enemies to mind flayers and cloakers, and hunt them when the opportunity presents itself.
Source: Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn p. 257

monster.spells: Command, Dissonant Whispers, Faerie Fire
monster.description:
Dragons of Caverns and Secrets Treasure: Arcana
Deep dragons slither through the wet and lightless places of the Underdark. They are stealthy hunters with an affinity for lost lore and fungi that flourish in the depths. As deep dragons age, their smooth, serpentine bodies become riddled with fungal rot, particularly around their faces, to imbue their breath with terror-inducing spores. Deep dragons covet treasure and knowledge. Some deep dragons seek to gain knowledge via experience and travel, slithering through caverns and seas of the Underdark to map hidden passages for dozens of miles. Other deep dragons enjoy cultivating groves of molds and fungi, including colossal varieties sufficient to conceal the dragons sinuous forms. Many deep dragons collect forgotten tomes or works of art and bully, cajole, or steal collections from drow or duergar sages. Deep dragons are excellent swimmers. They often clash with aquatic Underdark societies, such as kuotoa. Many deep dragons demand tribute from these groups in the form of food or treasure. Underdark explorers have many reasons to brave deep dragon lairs beyond treasure hunting; they might contain the only surviving copies of forgotten lore, fungal ingredients for cures or plagues, or maps to lost Underdark locales.
Young Deep Dragon: Young deep dragons establish lairs in familiar hunting grounds and defend their lairs with twisting passages and traps such as deadfalls. They dominate the local environment, consuming vast quantities of fish and pale crabs and cultivating fungal growths. They bully nearby communities when they can or enter into cautious arrangements with powerful Underdark settlements, such as drow cities.
Deep dragons, also called purple dragons, drakes of the depths, and silent hunters, are a type of chromatic dragon that lives in the Underdark.
Description: Despite their large size, deep dragons are slender and agile, and their snakelike bodies, narrow wings, and thin limbs allow them to crawl through the tunnels of the Underdark. Their scales are smooth, and in the light, an adult dragon's scales are the color of amethyst, while in the dark, they appear nearly black. In general, older specimens have much darker scales, while younger ones have more purple or maroon coloration. Older deep dragons are known to develop fungal growths around their heads and necks.
A dragon egg can be identified as that of a deep dragon by the purple tinge seen when held in front of an intense white light, though it shares this trait with shadow dragon and amethyst dragon eggs.
Personality: Deep dragons are patient and cunning. They prioritize their own survival above all else, yet are known to relish the opportunity to hunt or even fight if the situation demands it. They prefer to manipulate and negotiate rather than to risk combat, and are crafty dealmakers. They are quick to disregard any creature that isn't useful to them.
Deep dragons collect trivia, insights, tricks, and knowledge from far flung places, and delight in acquiring new information. They are known to collect magic items, not simply to hoard but also to use for themselves. Some deep dragons enjoy assuming the form of drow and infiltrating the dark elves' cities in disguise.
Abilities: In order to better allow them to navigate the narrow underground tunnels which they call home, deep dragons develop potent innate magical powers, including the ability to transmute rock to mud, and to cast spells like passwall, freedom of movement, and stone shape.
Perhaps their most distinctive ability is their unique shapechanging power which develops as they age. The first form they learn to adopt is that of a winged snake, which does not reduce their overall size but allows them to slither and fly unimpeded by extra limbs. The second form they learn to adopt is that of a normal humanoid, and they can alter this form's appearance as with a polymorph self spell.
Deep dragons are incapable of becoming intoxicated.
Combat: The claws of a deep dragon are intended to dig through solid rock, and as such, are devastating in combat even against heavily armored enemies. They prefer to pick off their enemies strategically, stalking them in the dark before pouncing or triggering a rockfall to bury them.
A deep dragon's breath weapon attacks creatures' minds, and causes the target to be dazed or dominated, depending on the strength of the wyrm. These effects are attributed to fungal spores that the dragon exhales. They are also known to be able to breathe a cone of gas that is caustic to flesh. Deep dragons are harmed by direct sunlight.
Ecology: Purple dragons inhabit the Underdark, and are rarely known on the surface. However, younger specimens are known to occasionally venture upward, generally with some mission to claim a treasure or exact revenge on a foe, but sometimes just for the sake of exploration. Young deep dragons rarely leave the lairs of their parents until they have mastered both their serpentine and humanoid alternative forms. Lairs are located in the Upperdark and Middledark, usually no deeper than 7 miles (11 kilometers), and are highly idiosyncratic: some are built within ancient ruins, others on the shores of underground lakes, and others are carved out of masses of living fungus. Regardless, most of these lairs are full of secret passages to allow the dragon to make quick escapes and to prepare surprise ambushes. Lairs are often difficult to access, even for the dragon itself without using its serpentine or humanoid form, and are filled with traps and servants to protect the dragon's hoard, especially for times when the dragon ventures out to seek new information or treasures. They are known to transplant dangerous specimens of fungi into their lairs to serve as traps, and in general, underground varietals of fungi often abound around deep dragons' lairs and even on their bodies. Their magic, and this somewhat symbiotic relationship with underground fungus, is said to be a result of their species' exposure to the pervading magic of the Underdark.
Diet: Deep dragons prefer "seafood" including clams, fish, kuo-toa, and even aboleths. That said, they are known to eat nearly anything, and it is not uncommon for Underdark societies to trade with a deep dragon by offering them food in the form of humanoid prisoners.
Uses: The claw of a deep dragon can be used as a special component in the casting of the dragon blight spell. Their scales are also highly-prized by drow wizards, used in the formation of their everdark ink.
Society: Deep dragons value and hoard knowledge, and prefer to collect unique treasures with interesting backstories. They meticulously organize their hoards, even framing or displaying their favorite pieces, and they delight in giving long tours to guests, particularly other deep dragons. While some actively avoid revealing themselves to other types of dragons, most enjoy their company. Deep dragons tend to look down on "inferior" creatures, but can be encountered near drow cities working as guardians for the drow, expecting to be paid for their services with a steady supply of food in the form of captives and criminals. However, other drow cities are highly distrustful and fearful of deep dragons. The drow of Menzoberranzan actively hunt down any deep dragon they learn of, and this in turn leads a group of four nearby deep dragons to plot against the city. They regularly visit the city under shapeshifted disguise, noting the weaknesses of the drow and opportune prey among the visitors of the city Bazaar. They are not above working with non-dragons, but treat them either as servants or subordinates. They are enemies to mind flayers and cloakers, and hunt them when the opportunity presents itself.
Source: Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn p. 257

monster.name: Adult Deep Dragon [5.5e]
monster.speed: Walk 40 ft., Burrow 30 ft., Fly 80 ft., Swim 40 ft.

trait.name: Legendary Resistance (3/Day, or 4/Day in Lair)
trait.text: If the dragon fails a saving throw, it can choose to succeed instead.

action.name: Multiattack
action.text: The dragon makes three Rend attacks.

action.name: Rend
action.text: Melee Attack Roll: +9, reach 10 ft. Hit: 14 (2d8+5) Slashing damage plus 5 (1d10) Poison damage.

action.name: Nightmare Breath (Recharge 5-6)
action.text: Wisdom Saving Throw: DC 15, each creature in a 30-foot Cone. Failure: 38 (7d10) Psychic damage, and the target has the Frightened condition until the end of the dragon's next turn. Success: Half damage only.

action.name: Spellcasting
action.text:
The deep dragon casts one of the following spells, requiring no Material components and using Charisma as the spellcasting ability (spell save DC 16):
• 1/day each: Command, Dissonant Whispers, Faerie Fire, Water Breathing

action.name: Shape-Shift (Bonus Action)
action.text: The dragon shape-shifts into a Small or Medium Humanoid or a Small or Medium Beast, or it returns to its true form. Its game statistics, other than its size, are the same in each form. Any equipment it is wearing or carrying isn't transformed.

legendary.name: Legendary Actions (4/Turn)
legendary.text: Legendary Actions Uses: 3/Turn, or 4/Turn in Lair Immediately after another creature's turn, the dragon can expend a use to take one of the following actions. The dragon regains all expended uses at the start of each of its turns.

legendary.name: Pounce
legendary.text: The dragon moves up to half its Speed, and it makes one Rend attack.

legendary.name: Spore Salvo
legendary.text: Constitution Saving Throw: DC 15, one creature within 30 feet of the dragon that it can see. Failure: 13 (3d8) Poison damage, and the target has the Poisoned condition. It repeats the save at the end of each of its turns, ending the effect on itself on a success. After 1 minute, it succeeds automatically. Failure or Success: The dragon can't take this action again until the start of its next turn.

legendary.name: Deep Dragon Lairs
legendary.text:
The region containing an adult or ancient deep dragon's lair is changed by its presence, creating the following effects:
• Preservation of Knowledge: Books and other written forms of communication with 1 mile of the lair become magically protected and can't be damaged by nonmagical means.
• Restless Sleep: When a creature finishes a Long Rest within 1 mile of the lair, the creature makes a DC 10 Constitution saving throw. On a failed save, the creature doesn't reduce its Exhaustion level as a result of finishing that Long Rest. Creatures with Immunity to the Poisoned condition are immune to this effect.
• Verdant Growth: Vegetation and fungi within 1 mile of the dragon's lair grow faster and cover a greater area than normal. Foraging in this area yields twice the usual amount of food. The dragon is immediately aware of the presence of any creature that eats this enhanced vegetation.
If the dragon dies or moves its lair elsewhere, these effects end immediately.

monster.name: Drow of Lolth [5.5e]

trait.name: Gear
trait.text: Chain Shirt, Hand Crossbow, Rapier Drow often wear magic armor and carry magic weapons that lose their enhancement bonuses permanently if they are exposed to sunlight for 1 hour or longer. A drow wearing a +1 chain shirt and carrying a +1 rapier has AC 16 and a +1 bonus on attack and damage rolls with rapier attacks.

trait.name: Fey Ancestry
trait.text: The drow has Advantage on saving throws it makes to avoid or end the Charmed condition, and magic can't put the drow to sleep.

trait.name: Sunlight Sensitivity
trait.text: While in sunlight, the drow has Disadvantage on attack rolls.

action.name: Rapier
action.text: Melee Attack Roll: +4, reach 5 ft. Hit: 6 (1d8+2) Piercing damage.

action.name: Drow Hand Crossbow
action.text: Ranged Attack Roll: +4, range 30/120 ft. Hit: 4 (1d4+2) Piercing damage and the target must make a DC 12 Constitution Saving Throw. Failure: The target has the Poisoned condition for 1 hour. If the target fails the save by 5 or more, it also has the Unconscious condition while Poisoned in this way. The target wakes up if it takes damage or if a creature within 5 feet of it takes an action to wake it.

action.name: Spellcasting (1/Day)
action.text:
The drow casts one of the following spells, requiring no Material components and using Charisma as the spellcasting ability (spell save DC 11):
• At will: Dancing Lights • 1/Day: Faerie Fire

monster.spells: Dancing Lights, Faerie Fire
monster.description:
Drow of Lolth: Elves Who Serve the Spider Queen Treasure: Any
Throughout the vast Underdark, in cities such as Menzoberranzan, many drow worship Lolth, the Spider Queen. Exiled from the surface world millennia ago, these drow now consider the Underdark to be their true home. Their insidious schemes include raiding the surface, plotting against each other, and preparing for ultimate war.
Drow of Lolth: Drow of Lolth defend cities in the Underdark and raid the surface in the name of the Spider Queen.
Description: Tens of thousands of years ago, the elves were divided, with those of benevolent disposition battling those that were selfish and cruel. The war among elvenkind ended when the good elves banished their malevolent kin to the subterranean depths. Here, in the lightless caverns and endless warrens of twisting passages, the dark elves-the drow-found refuge. They also found leadership in the only elven deity who had not forsaken them. At her command, the dark elves built an empire in the underworld.
Children of Lolth: The drow worship Lolth, a deity who resides in the Abyss. Known as the Spider Queen or the Demon Queen of Spiders, she is the figure around which the dark elves have built their subterranean civilization. Whatever she demands, the drow do. The wickedest of elves, drow are seldom seen by the surface world. Though they plot to destroy the elves that banished them, they no longer see themselves as exiles. They are the destined rulers of the darkness, and when Lolth commands them to rise up and destroy their surface-dwelling kin, they will.
Creatures of Darkness: The drow have lived underground for so long that they have evolved to their surroundings and can see in the dark. However, they can no longer stand sunlight. When slaves are in short supply in the Underdark, the drow send raiding parties to the surface to capture humanoids under cover of darkness, bringing them back to their cities to be tortured into submission. Beyond those occasional excursions, the drow are content to remain in their subterranean realm, where they feel secure and in control.
Underdark Cities: The dark elves build fantastic cities in enormous caverns where food and water are abundant. Their ability to sculpt stone rivals that of the greatest dwarf artisans, yet their structures retain a decidedly elven aesthetic. Though appearing delicate, drow settlements are structurally sound and remarkably resilient. The drow like to hollow out enormous stalagmites and stalactites, creating populated spires that rise from the floors and ceilings. A drow city is a sprawling metropolis enclosed by high walls. Non-drow visitors must conduct their business outside the walls under watchful eyes. The drow raise and keep giant spiders to help protect their cities against intruders, even as they drape those cities in beautiful webbing, creating a gossamer snare to catch flying enemies that would otherwise soar over the walls.
Drow Magic: Just as the drow have adapted to underground life, so too has their magic. In addition to using that magic to carve their cities from stone, they empower their weapons, create dangerous new magic items, and summon demons from the Abyss. Drow spellcasters are supremely arrogant and never hesitate to use their magic in the most abhorrent ways.
Arms and Armor: Drow craft weapons made of adamantine, a dark and supernaturally hard metal. Drow artisans adorn their weapons and armor with web-like filigree and spider motifs, and mages sometimes imbue items with magic to enhance their effectiveness. However, such magic fades when exposed to sunlight, so that magical drow weapons and armor rarely retain their enhancement bonuses and magical properties when brought to the surface.
Cutthroat Politics: Drow politics are cutthroat and rife with intrigue. When drow work together, it is typically to destroy a common foe and ensure their own survival, and such alliances are short lived and fraught with peril. Drow society is divided into noble houses, each ruled by a matron who seeks to raise the prestige and power of her house above all others. Other high-ranking members of the house are blood relatives, while the middling ranks are flush with drow from weaker families that have sworn fealty to the greater house. Clinging precariously to the bottom rung of a house's social ladder are the house slaves, made up of drow of low birth and the occasional non-drow captive.
Matriarchal Rule: Lolth, through her faithful priestesses, dictates the rules of drow society, ensuring that her orders and plots are carried out. Since Lolth is prone to manifesting on the Material Plane and directly punishing those that disobey her, the drow have learned to heed what she says and do as her priestesses command. In drow society, males are subservient to females. A male drow might lead an Underdark patrol or a raiding party to the surface, but he reports to a female drow-either the matron of his house or one of her hand-picked female subordinates. Although male drow can fill almost any function in drow society, they can't be priests, nor can they rule a house.
Poison Predilection: Distilled from spider venom and the flora of the Underdark, poison can be found in abundance among the drow, and it plays an important part in their culture and politics. Drow mages concoct a viscid toxin that leaves enemies unconscious. Drow warriors coat their blades and crossbow bolts with this venom, looking forward to the interrogation and torture that follows combat.
Source: Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn p. 260
