monster.description:
Nimblewrights: Cunningly Crafted Clockwork Sentinels Habitat: Urban; Treasure: None
Nimblewrights are fabricated from durable wood and animated by magic and clockwork gears. Some nimblewrights bear metal plates to protect their cogs and springs, while others have their workings exposed. No mere automatons, nimblewrights can form rudimentary plans and adapt their routines to account for dangers. Nimblewrights are surprisingly dexterous for creations made of animated wood and metal. A nimblewright walks with a flowing grace and fights with whirling pirouettes. Nimblewrights can serve as interesting background flavor in Calimshan or other areas where they are common. Roll or choose a result from the Nimblewright Tasks table as inspiration for what a nimblewright guard or nimblewright hulk might be doing in a busy public place.
Nimblewright Tasks: 1d6 | The Nimblewright Is ... 1 | Serving as an attentive bodyguard to a haughty dignitary. 2 | Scouting an area for a pending assassination. 3 | Seeking a thief that has stolen one of the nimblewright's cogs. 4 | Working to put out a fire before it spreads. 5 | Detaining a prisoner who claims innocence. 6 | Hauling mundane goods, but it is lost.
Nimblewright Guard: Nimblewright Guards are humanoid-shaped constructs that are typically employed as bodyguards, assassins, or spies. Watchful sentries that patrol important sites, nimblewright guards serve as loyal soldiers or work as vigilant bodyguards.
Combat Tactics: • Concealed Weapons: They fight with two built-in rapiers that fold into their forearms and can deploy instantly. • When disguised with clothing and magic, they can easily pass for any humanoid creature of similar size.
Notable Nimblewright Guards: • Nim, a particularly creative nimblewright who lived in the House of Inspired Hands. It was capable of creating other nimblewrights and had developed a nimblewright detector. • The Rogue: Out of loneliness and boredom, Nim secretly built a second nimblewright. This second construct fled the temple and eventually found its way into the service of the corrupt noble Yalah Gralhund, becoming an assassin.
Description: Nimblewrights are are built from wood, metal, magic, and clockwork.
Personality: Nimblewrights are created with intelligence, and each possesses a distinct, though chaotic, personality. This allows for more intuitive thinking and creativity than most other constructs are capable of.
• Rogue Actions: Nimblewrights are sometimes manipulated by nefarious nobles. For example, a rogue nimblewright was once hired by the Gralhund family to assassinate a gnome, accidentally triggering a deadly fireball explosion in Trollskull Alley.
Moral and Legal Status: In cities like Waterdeep, nimblewrights are strictly viewed as property with no inherent rights. City guards generally do not intervene if a nimblewright is destroyed or goes on a rampage, which often creates philosophical dilemmas for adventurers navigating the ethics of construct sentience.
Creation: Nimblewrights were originally created by ingenious artificers, and the procedure to create one is demanding in terms of money and power. • The creator has to know the spells geas, haste, wish, and polymorph. • Creating the body of a nimblewright requires approximately 500 pounds (230 kilograms) of flexible, precious metal alloys, and requires the creator to know either sculpting or masonry to shape. • Making the body costs about 15,000 gold pieces; the ritual as whole can cost up to 35,000 gold total. • Like golems, nimblewrights are created by binding an elemental ― in the case of a nimblewright, a water elemental ― to the artificial body and binding it to the creator's will.
History: In the late 15th century DR, numerous nimblewrights constructed in Lantan existed in Waterdeep. Four of them worked at the Sea Maidens Faire, under the command of Jarlaxle. Jarlaxle Baenre sold them cheaply because he embedded secret scrying crystals in them, allowing him to record everything the constructs see and hear.
Source: Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn p. 266

action.text: Ranged Attack Roll: +7, range 60 ft. Hit: 14 (4d6) Radiant damage.

monster.description:
Nimblewright Hulk: Nimblewright Hulks are heavy-duty, four-armed clockwork warriors. They are designed to be towering, heavily-plated brutes. While their bulk and steel armor fool enemies into thinking they are slow and dim-witted, they retain the signature agility of standard nimblewrights. The Hulk is an oversized, multi-armed variation engineered explicitly for heavy melee combat.
Combat Tactics: • Deceptive Speed: Because of their heavy steel plating, foes expect them to be lumbering behemoths, but their internal clockwork allows for lightning-fast, dexterous movements. • Halting Slams: In battle, their massive four-armed frames dish out devastating strikes that can completely stop a target's movement, making it deadly for adventurers attempting to flee.
Regional Lore: These arcane automatons are often used as high-end guards or as shock troops. You will frequently encounter or hear about them enforcing the will of wealthy nobles, powerful wizards, or genies.
Description: Nimblewrights are are built from wood, metal, magic, and clockwork.
Personality: Nimblewrights are created with intelligence, and each possesses a distinct, though chaotic, personality. This allows for more intuitive thinking and creativity than most other constructs are capable of. • Rogue Actions: Nimblewrights are sometimes manipulated by nefarious nobles. For example, a rogue nimblewright was once hired by the Gralhund family to assassinate a gnome, accidentally triggering a deadly fireball explosion in Trollskull Alley.
Moral and Legal Status: In cities like Waterdeep, nimblewrights are strictly viewed as property with no inherent rights. City guards generally do not intervene if a nimblewright is destroyed or goes on a rampage, which often creates philosophical dilemmas for adventurers navigating the ethics of construct sentience.
Creation: Nimblewrights were originally created by ingenious artificers, and the procedure to create one is demanding in terms of money and power.
• The creator has to know the spells geas, haste, wish, and polymorph. • Creating the body of a nimblewright requires approximately 500 pounds (230 kilograms) of flexible, precious metal alloys, and requires the creator to know either sculpting or masonry to shape. • Making the body costs about 15,000 gold pieces; the ritual as whole can cost up to 35,000 gold total. • Like golems, nimblewrights are created by binding an elemental ― in the case of a nimblewright, a water elemental ― to the artificial body and binding it to the creator's will.
History: In the late 15th century DR, numerous nimblewrights constructed in Lantan existed in Waterdeep. Four of them worked at the Sea Maidens Faire, under the command of Jarlaxle. Jarlaxle Baenre sold them cheaply because he embedded secret scrying crystals in them, allowing him to record everything the constructs see and hear.
Source: Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn p. 267

monster.name: Nimblewright Steed [5.5e]
monster.languages: Understands Common plus one other language but can't speak

trait.name: Evasion
trait.text: If the nimblewright is subjected to an effect that allows it to make a Dexterity saving throw to take only half damage, it instead takes no damage if it succeeds on the save and only half damage if it fails, provided it doesn't have the Incapacitated condition.

action.name: Hooves
action.text: Melee Attack Roll: +6, reach 5 ft. Hit: 7 (1d8+3) Bludgeoning damage. If the nimblewright moved at least 20 feet straight toward the target immediately before the hit, the target takes an extra 4 (1d8) Bludgeoning damage and, if it is Huge or smaller, has the Prone condition.

action.name: Nimble Movement (Bonus Action)
action.text: The nimblewright takes the Disengage action.

monster.description:
Nimblewright Steed: A Nimblewright Steed is a magical, clockwork construct fashioned by wealthy Faerûnian nobility as a mechanical mount. Unlike living animals, these constructs possess inexhaustible stamina but are notoriously quirky, often exhibiting an obsessive, programmed fixation on rigidly following a well-traveled road. The Steed serves as the primary mount used by a Nimblewright Guard.

monster.name: Phaerimm Hatchling [5.5e]
monster.languages: Telepathy 30 ft., Understands Common and Deep Speech but can't speak

trait.name: Magic Resistance
trait.text: The phaerimm has Advantage on saving throws against spells and other magical effects.

action.name: Multiattack
action.text: The phaerimm makes two Stinger attacks.

action.name: Stinger
action.text: Melee Attack Roll: +3, reach 5 ft. Hit: 3 (1d4+1) Piercing damage.

action.name: Spellcasting
action.text:
The phaerimm casts one of the following spells, requiring no spell components and using Charisma as the spellcasting ability (spell save DC 12):
• At will: Detect Thoughts, Mage Hand

monster.spells: Detect Thoughts, Mage Hand
monster.description:
Phaerimm: Alien, Magic-Obsessed Manipulators Treasure: Arcana, Implements
Phaerimm are malevolent alien beings that seek to dominate other sentient species. A phaerimm's conical body ripples through the air, trailing behind a large, flat mouth ringed by four delicate arms. A phaerimm's body tapers to a venomous stinger they prefer to use only when magical means fail them. Ancient phaerimm devastated the once-powerful empire of Netheril. The phaerimm were imprisoned beneath the great desert of Anauroch, where they plot a return to their former dominion. Roll or choose a result from the Phaerimm Plots table as inspiration for what a phaerimm agent might be doing when encountered.
Phaerimm Plots: 1d6 | The Phaerimm Is ... 1 | Searching for the pieces to a shattered, rune-encrusted iron plate. 2 | I Subtly twisting a small village's denizens to its will by masquerading as a benevolent, mysterious entity. 3 | Seeking a secure place for several phaerimm hatchlings to mature. 4 | Zealously guarding an Uncommon magic item that bears Netherese markings. 5 | Tormenting a wizard's hapless apprentice to extract magical knowledge. 6 | Preparing a ritual to summon trapped phaerimm from their nearby place of imprisonment.
Phaerimm Hatchling: Phaerimm hatchlings are parasitic aberrations born inside paralyzed, sentient hosts. At birth, they chew their way out and immediately possess innate magical abilities, casting spells as sorcerers. Phaerimms, also known as magicgrubs and thornbacks, are malevolent and highly intelligent aberrations who are natural spell-casters.
Description: Phaerimms are conical in shape with ovoid heads. They have barbed teeth and a venomous hollow barb on the end of their tails. Phaerimms have four arms. Their spiked, slug-shaped bodies are a greenish color covered by rough, scaly, and leathery hides.
Personality: Wholly evil and sadistic, phaerimms are ambitious and malicious creatures that work only for their own individual causes. They delight in bringing pain to others and would gladly erase all other beings from existence, save for the fact that they would lack slaves to torture for sport if they did so. Their thought processes and values are wholly alien to most other races; however, their inclination toward cruelty has the effect of making them somewhat predictable.
Combat: In addition to their spell-casting abilities, phaerimms are formidable opponents in melee combat. Their tail is strong enough to knock over most humanoids. The stinger at the end of the tail injects a powerful venom into a target, causing paralysis. They use their four arms to great effect in combat. Each arm is able to wield a weapon independently. A common tactic used by phaerimms in combat is to simply grab an opponent to drag to their tooth-covered maws, delivering a usually fatal bite. Despite these many strengths, most phaerimms feel that physical combat is only a last resort, and to engage in it is to admit that their magic is too weak to deal with a threat.
Abilities: Phaerimms are incredibly powerful spell-casters. Not only are they capable of casting far more spells than most human mages, they have developed their own unique spells, which can only be cast by phaerimms. They specialize in mind-controlling spells, which are so strong that they can control nearly any creature, including powerful ones such as beholders and mind flayers. A negative side-effect of phaerimm magic is that it drains moisture from the surrounding area. Extensive use of this magic led to the creation of the infamous Anauroch desert. All spells cast by a phaerimm are done through will alone; they do not require spell components or incantations. Their magical studies mainly compose of altering spells cast by humanoids to be cast in such a way. Phaerimms have a degree of natural resistance to nearly all effects and spells. Additionally, they also have the natural ability to absorb or deflect any spell cast on them. Phaerimm also have the ability to detect any magic.
Society: Phaerimms are solitary creatures but always live near other phaerimms, both for protection and to gain pleasure from unleashing devious schemes on one another. A phaerimm always retains a retinue of enslaved creatures. On the rare occasions when a group of phaerimms are threatened, they form a WarGather at a strategically important location. Phaerimms communicate with one another non-verbally by varying the wind speeds around their bodies. The phaerimm language is so complex it is usually incomprehensible to other creatures. It sounds like the whispering of strange winds. With non-phaerimms, they communicate telepathically. They understand Common and know several other languages. They do not maintain direct relations with non-phaerimm organizations or realms, instead relying on magically-enslaved agents to do their bidding beyond their territory. Phaerimms have a particular hatred for tomb tappers, because of their immunity to phaerimm mind control.
Habitat: Phaerimms make their homes in fortified underground caves. Since this is where a phaerimm stores its magical items and spellbooks, they are defended by powerful magical traps, slaves, and spellfields. Most phaerimm live in the Buried Realms beneath Anauroch, but small groups live elsewhere, such as in the ruins of Myth Drannor or the beholder city of Ooltul.
Biology: Phaerimms always choose to fly unless prevented from doing so. Phaerimms are carnivores, capturing mammals and reptiles, sentient or not, and holding them as slaves until slaughtered for consumption. Phaerimms have to live in an area that has magic. This is a result of their unique digestive tract. Their stomach acid and intestines rely on the presence of magic to digest and absorb nutrients properly. Despite their windbag-like bodies, the bodies of phaerimms do include skeletons. A phaerimm reproduces by injecting an egg into a victim with the stinger on its tail. The egg hatches within the paralyzed victim, and the larva begins consuming the host alive from the inside. The larva can be killed safely only with the casting of a cure disease spell. Phaerimms are capable of seeing any astral, incorporeal, or invisible creature within 120 feet (37 meters). They are also able to see with darkvision to a distance of up to 160 feet (49 meters) away.
History: Phaerimms dated back to the Days of Thunder. The wizards of the sarrukh empire of Isstosseffifil battled the phaerimms, and although the Isstossef succeeded in driving the phaerimms deep into the Underdark, the massive ecological change resulting from their weavings of Art caused the Isstosseffifil empire to collapse. At one point during the Founding Time, it was rumored that the Mhaurlok Expanse, an area of the Northdark where chaotic energy and primal forces ran wild, was created as a result of an ancient battle between Delzoun and the phaerimms.
Age of Humanity: In −461 DR, in retaliation and for their own survival, the phaerimms developed a powerful spell that drained the life from Netherese lands and their floating cities. Unbeknownst to the Netherese, their enormous usage of magic was destroying the underground home of the entire phaerimm race, which depended on the inherent magic of nature to survive. This created barren wastelands where there once were lush fields and areas of wild magic. The chaotic effects of magics caused the arcanists of High Netheril to flee the empire for safer lands. Within the next half century, in −427 DR, the phaerimms used spells to bring down the floating cities of Lhaoda and Tith Tilendrothael, resulting in the other Netherese enclaves setting wards against this type of attack. Circa −450 DR, large-scale Netherese migration into the Savage Frontier began, when the effects of the phaerimms' lifedrain dweomers became apparent. Many of the arcanists of Low Netheril fled for the recently-established magocracy of Illusk. The absence of the arcanists caused civil unrest in Low Netheril, and the commoners fled their homes. As the empire found it more difficult to feed its people, the stress led to a series of wars; some were fought to keep the restless populace entertained, while others were fought to claim more arable land. In −354 DR, the arcanist Melathlar fled Netheril to Illusk. He sacrificed his life to power the spell that raised a great stone tower, walls, and powerful spellwards around the Netherese settlement to protect it from the phaerimms. Later that year, the first recorded clash between the phaerimms and sharns occurred. A few years later in −350 DR, three powerful phaerimm sorcerers known as the Triumvirate took over the beholder city of Ooltul. In −100 DR, Delzoun, the Northkingdom, met its end before the advancing phaerimms and other threats. Its citadels on the surface survived and stayed under dwarven control. The sharns finally defeated the phaerimms in the Year of the Closed Scroll, 329 DR, thus halting the spread of Anauroch. They imprisoned them behind the Sharn Wall beneath Anauroch, in the Buried Realms, which the phaerimms called the Phaerlin. In 1346 DR, a portal to Avernus was erected in the Burial Glen of Myth Drannor by Banites loyal to the High Imperceptor of Mulmaster but under the influence of Zhentarim agents and, by proxy, a cabal of alhoon living in the ruins. The alhoon had it erected so that the devils it spawned would prevent the local phaerimms from attacking the liches while they searched the city for magic.
Era of Upheaval: The phaerimm that dwelt within the ruined Myth Drannor and its Dwarven Dungeons were driven out of large portions of the city by agents of the Cult of the Dragon, along with their red dragon dracolich ally, Pelendralaar, in the Year of the Gauntlet, 1369 DR. Some two years later, Nightal 20, the Year of the Unstrung Harp, 1371 DR, the Sharn Wall was breached near the city of Evereska, unleashing the phaerimm to cause chaos in the lands outside. A united force of elves, allies from Waterdeep and the shades from Thultanthar, which returned to Faerûn days later at the beginning of following year, kept the phaerimm at bay. The Shadovar began hunting and destroying phaerimm immediately on their return. In Evereska, they erected a shadowshell that prevented the phaerimms' escape. An attack on Thultanthar by the Chosen of Mystra, however, prevented them both from confirming that all of the phaerimm living there had been killed and from looting what magic remained. Also in Year of Wild Magic, 1372 DR the Shadovar targeted the colony of phaerimm living in the ruins of Myth Drannor for destruction. In the following decades they led a campaign into the Buried Realms, claiming the majority of Phaerlin, including Ooltul, for the new Netheril. In Year of the Ageless One, 1479 DR the Shadovar declared the phaerimm of Toril extinct. At the same time, however, they had come to suspect that at least one corpse of a phaerimm remained intact within the Phaerimm Memory Spire in Netheril. This would prove to be a woeful underestimate when, during a battle over the Spire against the Bedine in the Year of Dwarvenkind Reborn, 1488 DR, a whole hive of phaerimm were awoken within the Spire and proceeded to once again drain the life of the Anauroch (which had been restored by the Netherese during the preceding century). While the phaerimm of the Memory Spire were able to unleash their magics on the world around them, they themselves remained confined to their tomb by the power of Mystra. Meanwhile, the Chosen of Mystra traveled to the old breach in the Sharnwall and sacrificed a piece of the essence of Mystra within themselves to reseal and strengthen the barrier, entrapping any pharimm who still dwelt beneath the Anauroch. In the years following the Second Sundering, it was known that a small number of phaerimm remained free to roam and terrorize Toril, a few had survived by fleeing to Abeir, and it was unknown if more still existed deep in their underground homeland.
Source: Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn p. 268

monster.name: Phaerimm Agent [5.5e]
monster.languages: Telepathy 120 ft., Understands Common and Deep Speech but can't speak.

trait.name: Magic Resistance
trait.text: The phaerimm has Advantage on saving throws against spells and other magical effects.

action.name: Multiattack
action.text: The phaerimm makes three attacks, using Dread Stinger or Mindwarp Ray in any combination.

action.name: Dread Stinger
action.text: Melee Attack Roll: +7, reach 5 ft. Hit: 7 (1d6+4) Piercing damage plus 13 (2d12) Poison damage.

action.name: Mindwarp Ray
action.text: Ranged Attack Roll: +7, range 120 ft. Hit: 13 (2d8+4) Psychic damage, and the target has the Charmed condition until the start of the phaerimm's next turn.

action.name: Spellcasting
action.text:
The phaerimm casts one of the following spells, requiring no spell components and using Charisma as the spellcasting ability (spell save DC 15):
• At will: Detect Magic, Detect Thoughts, Mage Hand • 1/day each: Clairvoyance, Major Image, Synaptic Static

action.name: Teleport (Bonus Action)
action.text: The phaerimm teleports up to 30 feet to an unoccupied space it can see.

reaction.name: Protective Magic (3/Day)
reaction.text: The phaerimm casts Counterspell or Shield in response to the spell's trigger, using the same spellcasting ability as Spellcasting.

monster.spells: Detect Magic, Detect Thoughts, Mage Hand, Clairvoyance, Major Image, Synaptic Static, Counterspell, Shield

monster.name: Polar Serpent [5.5e]

trait.name: Misty Slithering
trait.text: The serpent can move through a space as narrow as 1 inch without expending extra movement to do so.

action.name: Multiattack
action.text: The serpent makes one Bite attack and uses Constrict.

action.name: Bite
action.text: Melee Attack Roll: +6, reach 5 ft. Hit: 8 (1d8+4) Piercing damage plus 3 (1d6) Cold damage.

action.name: Constrict
action.text: Strength Saving Throw: DC 14, one Medium or smaller creature the snake can see within 10 feet. Failure: 3 (1d6) Bludgeoning damage plus 7 (2d6) Cold damage. The target has the Grappled condition (escape DC 14), and it has the Restrained condition until the grapple ends.

monster.description:
Ice serpents, also known as polar serpents, are a variety of air elemental encountered in cold and snowy climates.
Description: They are large but ephemeral creatures of cold. Ice serpents have no bodies, and are instead comprised of constantly moving, ice-cold air and mist. They are naturally invisible, but they can usually be seen thanks to snow, ice particles, and small stones that are picked-up by their windy forms as they move. Unlike most air elementals, not all ice serpents cannot fly, and instead move forward by propelling themselves along the ground, giving the appearance of writhing and slithering. However, others are able to fly and can pass through spaces as narrow as 1 inch (2.5 centimeters).
Behavior: They are stealthy and perceptive, although not particularly intelligent. Even so, they can understand the Primordial language (although they cannot communicate with it).
Combat: Ice serpents attack by wrapping themselves around a target, but instead of constricting as a physical snake would, they instead drain the heat from their prey. Their victims begin to go numb from the cold, and ultimately fall unconscious as the serpent proceeds to drain the last of their vital heat. They can instantly constrict any victim smaller than themselves within 10 feet (3 meters), and their powerful jaws are also bitingly cold. As creatures of pure cold air, they are difficult to injure with mundane weapons and are fully immune to any magical or mundane ice or cold, although they are highly susceptible to fire.
Ecology: Ice serpents feed upon the body heat of living, warm-blooded creatures. They hunt in snowy regions under the cover of fog or snowstorms.
Homelands: They dwell in cold places, mostly snowy arctic environs but also underground such as in the Underdark. They can be found in Icewind Dale and are known to inhabit the Sea of Moving Ice as well as other parts of the North as far south and east as the Trollmoors. They range further south during the cold winter months.
History: These elementals first appeared in Faerûn in the mid-to-late 14th century DR, and were thought to have been summoned by an evil cleric of Akadi who dwelt near the Ice Lakes in the Frozenfar.
Source: Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn p. 269

monster.name: Rusted Behemoth [5.5e]

action.name: Multiattack
action.text: The Rusted makes three attacks, using Slam or Rusted Shot Put in any combination.

action.name: Slam
action.text: Melee Attack Roll: +10, reach 10 ft. Hit: 20 (4d6+6) Bludgeoning damage.

action.name: Rusted Shot Put
action.text: Ranged Attack Roll: +10, range 60/240 ft. Hit: 15 (2d8+6) Bludgeoning damage, and the target has the Poisoned condition until the end of its next turn.

reaction.name: Rust-Riddled Hide
reaction.text: Trigger: The Rusted is hit by an attack roll that deals Bludgeoning, Piercing, or Slashing damage. Response: Constitution Saving Throw: DC 16, each creature of the Rusted's choice in a 5-foot Emanation originating from the Rusted. Failure: the target has the Poisoned condition until the end of the target's next turn.

monster.description:
Rusted: Construct Victims of a Supernatural Curse Treasure: Individual
The supernatural Rusting curse that pervades the Moonshae Isles manifests as a thin scrim of iron over a living creature's skin. This coarse iron rusts easily, turning the creature a sickly orange gray. Unchecked, this curse transforms the victim into a Rusted, an animated iron caricature of itself that sheds flakes of toxic rust. As the Rusting curse hardens the skin, it also hollows out the mind. Rusted creatures despise unspoiled nature and are compelled to destroy it when they can.
Rusted Behemoths: Colossal, corrupted terrors that can dissolve and devour both magical and non-magical metal with a single bite. A giant overtaken by the Rusting is a fearsome juggernaut, rending trees and hills in a mindless rage. Their tough, rusted skin turns away blades and arrows in a shower of toxic orange dust. Rusted behemoths enjoy despoiling the wilderness.
Rusted: The rusted are creatures that have succumbed to the magical disease known as the Rusting, and have transformed into semi-intelligent constructs driven to destroy nature and spread the curse that created them.
Description: Nearly any living creature can become rusted. They remain recognizable, but are made of an animate, rust-colored iron that sheds toxic flakes. Becoming rusted is believed to greatly increase a creature's lifespan, however most rusted grow steadily weaker with time as their bodies corrode. They eventually crumble into dust.
Personality: Rusted creatures' minds are hollowed out by their transformations. While they maintain some semblance of their old personalities and intelligence, including the ability to speak, they discard any formerly held values or traditions and some become prone to mindless rages. They are compelled to despoil and pillage the natural environment by an innate hatred for untouched nature and an innate joy in destroying it. Many abhor all living things.
Combat: Rusted are stronger and more powerful than they were before their transformations. Given their iron composition, rusted are unaffected by poison and fatigue, and they cannot be petrified. Larger creatures have skins so thick that weapons bounce off of them.
Society: Rusted are most often encountered along the coasts and in the forests of the Moonshae Isles where they can readily inflict harm on the natural environment. They are known to chop down forests, open old mines, poison wells, and dredge wetlands purely for the sake of causing ecological damage, although they are also motivated to harvest the treasures that they find along the way. Some have the mental capacity to lead others or to negotiate trade deals. On land, rusted humans, giants (known as behemoths), and beasts rampage through the forests and seek to spread the Rusting to moonwells. At sea, they outfit ships with rusty metal plates, turning them into mighty warships known as rusted hulks. Larger monsters, such as the draconic rusted wyrms, use their incredible powers to boil streams and oceans, destroying habitats and reefs. By the turn of the 16th century DR, they could be found pillaging the natural resources of Alaron, Moray, Oman's Isle, and Snowdown, or haunting the waters off the coast of Norland.
History: The Rusting appeared on the Moonshae Isle of Snowdown in the late 15th century DR, and as of the turn of the 16th century DR, a great many rusted (mostly Northlander berserkers) had banded together as raiders and pirates in service of Queen Forfallen. They operated out of Ruathym, where they actively recruited new aspiring rusted, but also had bases at Iron Keep and Farview, where they harvested resources to fuel their war machine.
Notable Rusted: • Axenwright, a pirate captain and self-proclaimed jarl of Iron Keep as of the turn of the 16th century DR. • Kel, a rusted Northlander berserker. • Renauta, who was better known as Queen Forfallen.
The Rusting: The Rusting is a magical disease and curse that has afflicted the Moonshae Isles from the late 15th century through the turn of the 16th century DR. It transforms plants into metal and creatures into constructs known as "rusted".
Acquisition: The Rusting is a manifestation of the harm experienced by the Earthmother, patron deity of the Moonshae Isles, when the isles' natural environment is destroyed, polluted, or raided. The Rusting manifests in areas where ecological damage is present and is actively harming the Earthmother, regardless of whether the damage is purposeful or an unintended by-product of civilization. Activities such as the overfishing of seas, clearcutting of forests, strip-mining of mountains, draining of wetlands, damming or redirecting of waterways, or general overpopulation, pollution, and industrialization can cause the Rusting to manifest. Creatures can contract the Rusting by being in close proximity to lands and waters afflicted by it, even for as little as a single hour, or if they are injured by a rusted creature. It can infect any living thing, not only humanoids and beasts but also including celestials, dragons, fey, giants, and monstrosities. Constructs and the undead are not affected by the curse. It is speculated that fomorians are somehow connected to the Rusting as they tend to emerge from the Underdark wherever the disease spreads.
Effects: The first signs of the Rusting are intense fatigue, hacking cough, and a thin, coarse plaque of iron that begins to grow over the body, starting around the eyes. This iron plaque plates the infected individual's joints and slows their movements. If exposed to any moisture, the iron rusts quickly into a gray and orange metallic coating. As it spreads over the following days, the fatigue and exhaustion become more acute. After as little as six days, the victim can succumb to the disease as their body turns to animate iron and their mind is destroyed. At this point, they have become a "rusted" version of themselves, and are compelled to despoil or ravage the natural environment around them, thus perpetuating the curse. Eventually, rusted creatures crumble into dust.
Environment: The Rusting transforms green vegetation into scrap metal and dust. Trees whiten and die or else become covered in iron with their leaves turning to rust. The curse can rapidly spread over wooden structures and causes rocks to disintegrate. Contaminated waterways develop a metallic smell and rust-colored tint. If the Rusting manifests in open water, it creates a phenomenon known as a rusted sea where the water is coated in a thin oil that has a foul chemical smell and is hazardous to aquatic creatures. These areas can drive whales to beach themselves and are attractive to rusted sea monsters. If a moonwell becomes contaminated, it transforms into a glistening and stinking pool of black oil, which injures the Earthmother as a bleeding wound would injure a mortal. The spread of the curse causes the goddess constant suffering. Aberrations and undead tend to be common in places affected by the Rusting. While the connection between these monsters and the curse is unclear, places suffused by the curse seem to spawn these monsters.
Treatment: Infected creatures and individuals can be cured of the Rusting by removing the curse (e.g., via the remove curse spell). It is also possible to fight off the disease naturally. However, it is irreversible once the victim has transformed into a rusted. Rusted wooden structures, such as ships, can be burned to prevent the curse from spreading. The Rusting is known to disappear from lands and waters where environmental damage is addressed or reversed. This might require cleaning up or ceasing polluting activities or halting lumbering operations. Druids are said to be able to protect places against the Rusting if they are able to directly tend to them, and they work alongside rangers to keep moonwells safe from the contagion.
History: The Rusting was foretold by a satyr seer in ancient Sarifal approximately two thousand years before it manifested. This prophecy claimed that a "mysterious curse" or "howling disease" would be spread by a "beast lord" and could destroy "two worlds" unless High Lady Ordalf of Sarifal died to stop it. The prophecy was sufficient to frighten Ordalf into fleeing the Material Plane for centuries, with her only returning when she sensed that the time for her necessary sacrifice was approaching. The curse echoed and perpetuated the ecological damage that had been perpetrated by Amnian colonists on the island of Snowdown throughout most of the 15th century DR. Their decades-long resource extraction activities had been hugely polluting, from digging mining pits to cutting down forests to contaminating ponds and redirecting waterways into polluted wetlands, all of which were overseen by the vampire Erliza Daressin. The Amnians were finally driven out in the 1480s DR when the forces of House Kendrick and Sarifal allied against them, however when Princess Tarilyn Kendrick slew Lady Daressin, the vampire used her last breath to utter a curse that sparked the Rusting. The Rusting first appeared at the only moonwell on Snowdown, which had long been abandoned after the Amnians had driven off the druids who had once cared for it. Attempts to contain or repair the Rusting failed spectacularly, and the situation was made much worse when a dam burst along the Harloch, depositing pollution and runoff from the isle's mines all across the lowlands. Snowdown was soon regarded as little more than a blight on the Moonshaes. In the following decades, fomorians, rusted bandits, undead, and aberrant monsters stalked the island while famine gripped its remaining inhabitants. Peoples of the Moonshaes regarded the disease as insidious and strange, and it forced some folk to flee their homes. However, a few saw the transformation into a rusted as a chance to acquire power and longevity, and so intentionally committed violence against the land in hopes of spreading and acquiring the curse. As of the turn of the 16th century DR, many such individuals were followers of the pirate leader known as Queen Forfallen and had established bases for themselves at Iron Keep on Oman's Isle and Farview on Moray. From these sites, they chopped down forests, reopened old mines, and dredged wetlands, seeking to find treasures and to expand their pirate fleet of rusty ships. The Rusting also arrived on the island of Norland following years of pollution and overfishing of the Bay of Norland: at the port of Rogarsheim, the curse infused the water, infected ships, and spread across the timbers of the piers, occasionally ensnaring a dockworker. In the Year of the Shining Mythal, 1501 DR, deforestation, pollution, and use of alchemical fertilizers led the Rusting to appear on the southern shore of Alaron at Kythyss, where it spread from the town harbor up the Bregonshire coast and into Rushdown Wood, threatening a moonwell. It had also reached the Dernall Forest further north on the island, and from there, rust-tainted water had seeped into the Feywild. On Norland, the rusted Tvarstoldt tar pits in the Jotunhammer Mountains had begun to spawn foul monsters, and fomorians worked to thwart any attempts to heal the land. On Oman's Isle, the rusted pirate Axenwight strove to harvest the natural treasures and to corrupt the isle's moonwell. The only one of the Moonshaes where the Rusting had not yet arrived was Gwynneth, where the high concentration of moonwells meant that a Rusting outbreak could prove fatal to the Earthmother. Once it was clear that the Rusting was the disease that High Lady Ordalf was destined to stop, it became apparent that she would need to give her life to empower potent magic that could cure it.
Rumors and Legends: It is feared that a contaminated moonwell could be used to summon a terrible rusted form of Kazgaroth, who would be able to spread the curse instantly to anything it touched.
Source: Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn p. 272

trait.name: Gear
trait.text: Greatsword, 6 Javelins

action.name: Multiattack

monster.name: Rusted Wyrm [5.5e]

trait.name: Legendary Resistance (3/Day)
trait.text: If the Rusted fails a saving throw, it can choose to succeed instead.

action.name: Multiattack
action.text: The Rusted makes two Bite attacks.

action.name: Bite
action.text: Melee Attack Roll: +12, reach 20 ft. Hit: 29 (4d10+7) Piercing damage.

action.name: Steam Breath (Recharge 5-6)
action.text: Dexterity Saving Throw: DC 19, each creature and flammable object that isn't being worn or carried in a 60-foot Cone. Failure: 45 (7d12) Fire damage, and the target starts burning. action.name: Encasing Rust (Bonus Action)

It is speculated that fomorians are somehow connected to the Rusting as they tend to emerge from the Underdark wherever the disease spreads.
Effects: The first signs of the Rusting are intense fatigue, hacking cough, and a thin, coarse plaque of iron that begins to grow over the body, starting around the eyes. This iron plaque plates the infected individual's joints and slows their movements. If exposed to any moisture, the iron rusts quickly into a gray and orange metallic coating. As it spreads over the following days, the fatigue and exhaustion become more acute. After as little as six days, the victim can succumb to the disease as their body turns to animate iron and their mind is destroyed. At this point, they have become a "rusted" version of themselves, and are compelled to despoil or ravage the natural environment around them, thus perpetuating the curse. Eventually, rusted creatures crumble into dust.
Environment: The Rusting transforms green vegetation into scrap metal and dust. Trees whiten and die or else become covered in iron with their leaves turning to rust. The curse can rapidly spread over wooden structures and causes rocks to disintegrate. Contaminated waterways develop a metallic smell and rust-colored tint. If the Rusting manifests in open water, it creates a phenomenon known as a rusted sea where the water is coated in a thin oil that has a foul chemical smell and is hazardous to aquatic creatures. These areas can drive whales to beach themselves and are attractive to rusted sea monsters. If a moonwell becomes contaminated, it transforms into a glistening and stinking pool of black oil, which injures the Earthmother as a bleeding wound would injure a mortal. The spread of the curse causes the goddess constant suffering. Aberrations and undead tend to be common in places affected by the Rusting. While the connection between these monsters and the curse is unclear, places suffused by the curse seem to spawn these monsters.
Treatment: Infected creatures and individuals can be cured of the Rusting by removing the curse (e.g., via the remove curse spell). It is also possible to fight off the disease naturally. However, it is irreversible once the victim has transformed into a rusted. Rusted wooden structures, such as ships, can be burned to prevent the curse from spreading. The Rusting is known to disappear from lands and waters where environmental damage is addressed or reversed. This might require cleaning up or ceasing polluting activities or halting lumbering operations. Druids are said to be able to protect places against the Rusting if they are able to directly tend to them, and they work alongside rangers to keep moonwells safe from the contagion.
History: The Rusting was foretold by a satyr seer in ancient Sarifal approximately two thousand years before it manifested. This prophecy claimed that a "mysterious curse" or "howling disease" would be spread by a "beast lord" and could destroy "two worlds" unless High Lady Ordalf of Sarifal died to stop it. The prophecy was sufficient to frighten Ordalf into fleeing the Material Plane for centuries, with her only returning when she sensed that the time for her necessary sacrifice was approaching. The curse echoed and perpetuated the ecological damage that had been perpetrated by Amnian colonists on the island of Snowdown throughout most of the 15th century DR. Their decades-long resource extraction activities had been hugely polluting, from digging mining pits to cutting down forests to contaminating ponds and redirecting waterways into polluted wetlands, all of which were overseen by the vampire Erliza Daressin. The Amnians were finally driven out in the 1480s DR when the forces of House Kendrick and Sarifal allied against them, however when Princess Tarilyn Kendrick slew Lady Daressin, the vampire used her last breath to utter a curse that sparked the Rusting. The Rusting first appeared at the only moonwell on Snowdown, which had long been abandoned after the Amnians had driven off the druids who had once cared for it. Attempts to contain or repair the Rusting failed spectacularly, and the situation was made much worse when a dam burst along the Harloch, depositing pollution and runoff from the isle's mines all across the lowlands. Snowdown was soon regarded as little more than a blight on the Moonshaes. In the following decades, fomorians, rusted bandits, undead, and aberrant monsters stalked the island while famine gripped its remaining inhabitants. Peoples of the Moonshaes regarded the disease as insidious and strange, and it forced some folk to flee their homes. However, a few saw the transformation into a rusted as a chance to acquire power and longevity, and so intentionally committed violence against the land in hopes of spreading and acquiring the curse. As of the turn of the 16th century DR, many such individuals were followers of the pirate leader known as Queen Forfallen and had established bases for themselves at Iron Keep on Oman's Isle and Farview on Moray. From these sites, they chopped down forests, reopened old mines, and dredged wetlands, seeking to find treasures and to expand their pirate fleet of rusty ships. The Rusting also arrived on the island of Norland following years of pollution and overfishing of the Bay of Norland: at the port of Rogarsheim, the curse infused the water, infected ships, and spread across the timbers of the piers, occasionally ensnaring a dockworker. In the Year of the Shining Mythal, 1501 DR, deforestation, pollution, and use of alchemical fertilizers led the Rusting to appear on the southern shore of Alaron at Kythyss, where it spread from the town harbor up the Bregonshire coast and into Rushdown Wood, threatening a moonwell. It had also reached the Dernall Forest further north on the island, and from there, rust-tainted water had seeped into the Feywild. On Norland, the rusted Tvarstoldt tar pits in the Jotunhammer Mountains had begun to spawn foul monsters, and fomorians worked to thwart any attempts to heal the land. On Oman's Isle, the rusted pirate Axenwight strove to harvest the natural treasures and to corrupt the isle's moonwell. The only one of the Moonshaes where the Rusting had not yet arrived was Gwynneth, where the high concentration of moonwells meant that a Rusting outbreak could prove fatal to the Earthmother. Once it was clear that the Rusting was the disease that High Lady Ordalf was destined to stop, it became apparent that she would need to give her life to empower potent magic that could cure it.
Rumors and Legends: It is feared that a contaminated moonwell could be used to summon a terrible rusted form of Kazgaroth, who would be able to spread the curse instantly to anything it touched.
Source: Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn p. 273

action.name: Rend

action.name: Ruinous Breath (Recharge 5-6)
action.text: Constitution Saving Throw: DC 12, each creature in a 15-foot Cone. Failure: 13 (3d8) Necrotic damage. Success: Half damage.

monster.description:
Spirit Dragons: Draconic Scions of an Ancient Empire Treasure: Any
Spirit dragons, sometimes called song dragons, are powerful dragons whose powers stem from the magic and history of fallen realms. They embody the spirit of a bygone age, and so as they grow and mature, they develop an erratic control over time. A spirit dragon's primary motivation is to unearth and study the ruins of the ancient realm from which it arose. Spirit dragons share an innate intellectual curiosity, and many have a deep appreciation for the culture and art of humanoid societies. Spirit dragons find even the most commonplace melodies moving. A song written in the time and region from which a spirit dragon hails can potentially overwhelm the dragon, driving it to either morose despondence or passionate rage. No two spirit dragons are exactly alike; each individual bears features distinct to the empire from which it hails. Roll on or choose a result from the Spirit Dragon Origins table to determine which lost realm a spirit dragon is from.
Spirit Dragon Origins: 1d6 | The Spirit Dragon Traces Its Origins To... 1 | Evermeet, a mythical realm of the elves. 2 | Imaskar, a southern empire of artificers. 3 | Jhaamdath, a prehistoric psiocracy. 4 | Myth Drannor, a legendary city of magic. 5 | Netheril, an empire of arcane secrets. 6 | Ostoria, the first kingdom of the giants.
Spirit Dragon Wyrmling: When a dragon egg is found buried among ancient rubble and given the right conditions, a spirit dragon wyrmling might hatch from the egg. Left to its own devices, a wyrmling wanders the ruins that the dragon originated from.
Spirit dragons, sometimes known as song dragons, are unique and powerful dragons associated with the magic and memory of bygone ages and realms.
Description: A spirit dragon can hatch from any dragon egg buried in ancient ruins and left to incubate under certain conditions. Once hatched, they grow into living embodiments of the ancient place from which they originated. Each spirit dragon has distinct features that belie the lost realm or age with which they are associated, although all have wings with which to fly. From a young age, they can also burrow with surprising efficiency, assisted by their natural blindsight.
Personality: Spirit dragons are driven first and foremost by a hunger to learn about, understand, and unearth the secrets of the society that left the ruins in which their egg hatched. They spend their whole lives learning about this lost culture and its beliefs and outlook, and assimilate much of what they learn into their own personalities. On occasion, they are known to hire adventurers to delve into the ruins of their homelands. They further have a general innate appreciation for and curiosity about the intellectual, artistic, and cultural facets of other humanoid societies, particularly their music. While they find even mundane songs to be moving, they are struck with deep and potentially overwhelming emotions upon hearing a song written by the lost society with which they associate.
Combat: Spirit dragons draw their power from the very history and magic of ancient and lost places, which manifests as both limited and erratic control over time itself as well as necrotic energy that suffuses their physical attacks. They are in turn resistant to the effects of necrotic magic. They also master spellcasting as they age. Older dragons can cast detect magic, shapechange (although they are limited to animal or humanoid forms), and thunderwave whenever they wish and without any material components (and are known to make extensive use of thunderwave in battle). Once each day, they can also cast legend lore and sequester. One of the most remarkable abilities they develop in their adulthood is the magic to physically unearth ancient ruins and raise them into the air. They use this power in battle to bludgeon enemies with ancient stones or to disrupt the battlefield and hamper enemy movements.
Breath Weapon: Spirit dragons possess two distinct breath attacks. The first is a ruinous, 90‑foot-long (27‑meter) blast of necrotic power. The second warps time in a 90‑foot-long (27‑meter) cone, which can cause creatures to appear to be moving and reacting half as fast as normal.
Homelands: While spirit dragons can theoretically be found in any ancient ruins, they are notably said to inhabit places associated with the ancient empires of Imaskar, Jhaamdath, Netheril, and Ostoria, as well as other places with long histories like Evermeet or Myth Drannor. They are occasionally known to cause trouble in nearby regions if they experiment with hazardous forgotten magic or inadvertently unleash long-buried dangers.
Lairs: A spirit dragon generally makes its lair in a ruined monument or city nearby to the remains or remnants of the ancient realm with which it is obsessed. The dragon's presence within its lair causes all music to become more beautiful, all creatures to age at one-tenth their normal rate, and anyone aside from the dragon or its friends to be more susceptible to charm magics. The region within 1 mile (1,600 meters) of the lair comes under the influence of this magic for as long as the dragon dwells there.
Lifecycle: Wyrmlings spend their days exploring the ruins in which their egg hatched. As they gain confidence and mature, they begin delving into the ruins' secrets and testing ancient magics. As adults, they are known to travel in disguise (using the shapechange spell) amongst humanoids to indulge their curiosity. Finally, ancient specimens have spent so many centuries immersed in the study of their ancient homeland that their world view becomes identical to that of the long lost society's. At this point, they hold almost no remaining interest in the concerns of their current time and place.
Source: Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn p. 277

The dragon casts one of the following spells, requiring no spell components and using Intelligence as the spellcasting ability (spell save DC 18):
• At will: Detect Magic, Shapechange (Beast or Humanoid form only, no Temporary Hit Points gained from the spell, and no Concentration or Temporary Hit Points required to maintain the spell), Thunderwave • 1/day: Legend Lore (as an action)

action.text: Wisdom Saving Throw: DC 18, each creature that isn't currently affected by this breath in a 60-foot Cone. legendary.name: Legendary Actions (4/Turn)
legendary.text: Legendary Action Uses: 3/Turn, or 4/Turn in Lair. Immediately after another creature's turn, the dragon can expend a use to take one of the following actions. The dragon regains all expended uses at the start of each of its turns.

legendary.name: Pounce
legendary.text: The dragon moves up to half its Speed, and it makes one Rend attack.

legendary.name: Shattering Wave
legendary.text: The dragon uses Spellcasting to cast Thunderwave.

legendary.name: Unearth Ruins
legendary.text: The dragon magically raises broken, ancient ruins in a 20-foot-radius, 60-foot-high Cylinder centered on a point it can see within 120 feet. Ground in the Cylinder becomes Difficult Terrain. Each creature in the Cylinder when it appears is subjected to the following effect. Strength Saving Throw: DC 18. Failure: 5 (2d4) Bludgeoning damage, and the target has the Prone condition. Failure or Success: The dragon can't take this action again until the start of its next turn.

legendary.name: Spirit Dragon Lairs
legendary.text:
Spirit dragons haunt the ruined cities and buried monuments of ancient empires. The region containing an adult or ancient spirit dragon's lair is changed by its presence, creating the following effects:
Enchanted Acoustics: Creatures within 1 mile of the lair have Advantage on Charisma (Performance) checks that involve singing or playing music. Creatures other than the dragon and its allies in that area have Disadvantage on saving throws to avoid or end the Charmed condition.
Time Distortion: While within 1 mile of the lair, creatures age at one-tenth the usual rate.
If the dragon dies or moves its lair elsewhere, these effects end immediately.
