A song written in the time and region from which a spirit dragon hails can potentially overwhelm the dragon, driving it to either morose despondence or passionate rage. No two spirit dragons are exactly alike; each individual bears features distinct to the empire from which it hails. Roll on or choose a result from the Spirit Dragon Origins table to determine which lost realm a spirit dragon is from.
Spirit Dragon Origins: 1d6 | The Spirit Dragon Traces Its Origins To... 1 | Evermeet, a mythical realm of the elves. 2 | Imaskar, a southern empire of artificers. 3 | Jhaamdath, a prehistoric psiocracy. 4 | Myth Drannor, a legendary city of magic. 5 | Netheril, an empire of arcane secrets. 6 | Ostoria, the first kingdom of the giants.
Ancient Spirit Dragon: Ancient spirit dragons have outgrown the petty concerns of the current age. After centuries of studying the culture and beliefs of an ancient empire, a spirit dragon's personality and outlook are often indistinguishable from that fallen realm's.
Spirit dragons, sometimes known as song dragons, are unique and powerful dragons associated with the magic and memory of bygone ages and realms.
Description: A spirit dragon can hatch from any dragon egg buried in ancient ruins and left to incubate under certain conditions. Once hatched, they grow into living embodiments of the ancient place from which they originated. Each spirit dragon has distinct features that belie the lost realm or age with which they are associated, although all have wings with which to fly. From a young age, they can also burrow with surprising efficiency, assisted by their natural blindsight.
Personality: Spirit dragons are driven first and foremost by a hunger to learn about, understand, and unearth the secrets of the society that left the ruins in which their egg hatched. They spend their whole lives learning about this lost culture and its beliefs and outlook, and assimilate much of what they learn into their own personalities. On occasion, they are known to hire adventurers to delve into the ruins of their homelands. They further have a general innate appreciation for and curiosity about the intellectual, artistic, and cultural facets of other humanoid societies, particularly their music. While they find even mundane songs to be moving, they are struck with deep and potentially overwhelming emotions upon hearing a song written by the lost society with which they associate.
Combat: Spirit dragons draw their power from the very history and magic of ancient and lost places, which manifests as both limited and erratic control over time itself as well as necrotic energy that suffuses their physical attacks. They are in turn resistant to the effects of necrotic magic. They also master spellcasting as they age. Older dragons can cast detect magic, shapechange (although they are limited to animal or humanoid forms), and thunderwave whenever they wish and without any material components (and are known to make extensive use of thunderwave in battle). Once each day, they can also cast legend lore and sequester. One of the most remarkable abilities they develop in their adulthood is the magic to physically unearth ancient ruins and raise them into the air. They use this power in battle to bludgeon enemies with ancient stones or to disrupt the battlefield and hamper enemy movements.
Breath Weapon: Spirit dragons possess two distinct breath attacks. The first is a ruinous, 90‑foot-long (27‑meter) blast of necrotic power. The second warps time in a 90‑foot-long (27‑meter) cone, which can cause creatures to appear to be moving and reacting half as fast as normal.
Homelands: While spirit dragons can theoretically be found in any ancient ruins, they are notably said to inhabit places associated with the ancient empires of Imaskar, Jhaamdath, Netheril, and Ostoria, as well as other places with long histories like Evermeet or Myth Drannor. They are occasionally known to cause trouble in nearby regions if they experiment with hazardous forgotten magic or inadvertently unleash long-buried dangers.
Lairs: A spirit dragon generally makes its lair in a ruined monument or city nearby to the remains or remnants of the ancient realm with which it is obsessed. The dragon's presence within its lair causes all music to become more beautiful, all creatures to age at one-tenth their normal rate, and anyone aside from the dragon or its friends to be more susceptible to charm magics. The region within 1 mile (1,600 meters) of the lair comes under the influence of this magic for as long as the dragon dwells there.
Lifecycle: Wyrmlings spend their days exploring the ruins in which their egg hatched. As they gain confidence and mature, they begin delving into the ruins' secrets and testing ancient magics. As adults, they are known to travel in disguise (using the shapechange spell) amongst humanoids to indulge their curiosity. Finally, ancient specimens have spent so many centuries immersed in the study of their ancient homeland that their world view becomes identical to that of the long lost society's. At this point, they hold almost no remaining interest in the concerns of their current time and place.
Source: Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn p. 279

monster.name: Spore of Moander [5.5e]
monster.conditionImmune: Blinded, Deafened, Exhaustion, Paralyzed, Poisoned, Prone

trait.name: Explosive Core
trait.text: When the spore is subjected to Fire damage, each creature in a 5-foot Emanation originating from the spore takes 7 (2d6) Fire damage.

trait.name: Rolling Mass
trait.text: The spore doesn't need to expend extra movement to move through Difficult Terrain.

action.name: Multiattack
action.text: The spore makes four Tendril attacks. Alternatively, it makes two Tendril attacks and uses Consume once.

action.name: Tendril
action.text: Melee Attack Roll: +10, reach 20 ft. Hit: 11 (1d10+6) Piercing damage plus 10 (3d6) Acid damage. If the target is Large or smaller, the spore pulls the target 5 feet straight toward itself.

action.name: Consume
action.text: Strength Saving Throw: DC 18, one Large or smaller creature within 5 feet. Failure: The target is pulled into the spore's space and has the Grappled condition (escape DC 16). Until the grapple ends, the target has the Blinded and Restrained conditions, and it takes 17 (5d6) Acid damage at the start of each of the spore's turns. When the spore moves, the Grappled target moves with it, costing it no extra movement. The spore can have one Large creature or up to nine Medium or smaller creatures Grappled at a time.

monster.description:
Spore Of Moander: Hulking Heap of the Rotting God Treasure: None
A spore of Moander is a rotting mass of vegetation infused with the divine power of Moander, dead god of corruption and decay. Spores arise on the Material Plane where Moander's influence can still be felt: primordial swamps, ancient forests, and miasmic lagoons touched by Abyssal evil. A spore of Moander has no grand agenda beyond spreading death and sorrow. Still, cultists of Moander look on these terrible creatures with reverence, believing that each spore is a window into the unknowable mind of Moander.
The Spores of Moander are hulking heaps of Abyssal botanical horror related to the lore of Moander, the ancient dead god of rot and decay.
Lore: • Origins: The creature rises from primordial places contaminated by the foulest Abyssal evil. It has no grand goal other than to spread death, sorrow, and decay wherever it slithers or grows. • Combat Style: The Spore of Moander fights by consuming, grappling, and ensnaring foes with tendrils of rotting vegetation. It features powerful acidic attacks and an explosive core. • Swamp Dungeons: They are known to lurk in fetid swamps and forgotten undergrowth, perfect for wilderness survival encounters or traversing treacherous, rotting terrain. • The "Pod People" Plot: Cultists might implant seeds into humanoids or sacred creatures, creating bursting pods that spawn more of the corruption.
Moander: Moander (pronounced: /moʊɛˈɑːndɛr/ moe-AN-der) is an ancient deity of rot, corruption, and decay, whose origins predate the empire of Netheril. Some believe that the Darkbringer is an elder god. Despite being banished from Toril on many occasions, the Jawed God always slithers back.
Description: Moander has been depicted and described in ancient texts as a masculine deity, a feminine power, or simply referred to as "it." The Darkbringer's most renowned avatar is called the Abomination of Moander, a massive pile of animated rotting mass of animal carrion and putrified vegetation. The Abomination has some superficial resemblance to shambling mounds and gibbering mouthers. The entire surface of the avatar is covered in vines, lichen, moss, tendrils, eyes, and fanged maws of different shapes, sizes and belonging to different creatures. All mouths mumble, crack, screech, and emit deafening uncontrollable chaotic ravings and chant Moander's name in a demented chorus. The Abomination, a lumbering mountain of rot, produces putrid black slime, shedding it behind everywhere it goes. It absorbs any living or dead matter, increasing the Abomination's body size. This form is akin to that of a blob of annihilation.
Manifestations: Moander appears to his worshipers in an intangible image of a red-eyed giant rotting male humanoid head that sprouts 20 feet (6.1 meters) long tendrils instead of hair and has a maw filled with fangs. This manifestation allows Moander to communicate, manipulate objects with the tendrils, and create a mental link with the individuals the deity touches with the tentacles. The link remains even after the contact is broken, and the dark god continues whispering in the individuals' minds until the effects are negated via remove curse or remove disease spells. As the god of decay, Moander can manifest through any type of rot. The deity creates long tentacles of rotting matter that sprout from the spots of decay. Each tendril is 20 feet (6.1 meters) long and can freely manifest and move from one stop of rot to the next, within reach. These putrid tentacles can slam at the god's enemies and implant immobilized or sleeping creatures with the seed of Moander. These tendrils can feed on decaying matter, and after devouring enough, they sprout a bulb that matures into another independent tendril. These manifestations die and disintegrate when left without food after one-to-eight months.
Personality: The Darkbringer is a cruel deity who revels in controlling its subjects. The tyrant delights in the torment and destruction of lesser beings; it seeks to force mortals' hands to ruin those they hold dear. Moander seeks to corrupt anyone who refuses to bow down to it. The Jawed God uses lies and half-truths to cause emotional distress to those it tortures.
Powers: In his Abomination avatar shape, Moander is unable to cast spells. However, that is compensated by the sheer power and resilience of the creature. The rotting hulk can freely move across vertical surfaces or float on water. The entirety of its putrid mass can sprout tendrils, eyes, or mouths to communicate or to land devastating attacks on its enemies. Despite being an easy target, the Abomination of Moander has thick natural defenses, absorbing most attacks into its rotting mass. The Abomination has to be created by the hands of its servants, and the decaying mass that becomes the vessel of the Jawed God has to be at least 30 feet (9.1 meters) in diameter. The Abomination needs to continuously absorb organic matter in order to grow or simply exist. If left without access to new matter, the Abomination eventually rots away within one to four months and turns to dust and foul slime. The Abomination's main mode of attack is via tendril slams and sprouting a massive fanged maw that devours all who stand in front of the avatar. Moander's rotting body also often uses huge tree trunks as spear-like projectiles or entangles its enemies. The avatar can also implant the seed of Moander into captured living creatures, taking full control over them. Those who are unlucky enough to be swallowed by the Abomination are crushed as endless tendrils rot away their equipment and clothes, eventually killing them and adding the carcasses to Moander's avatar. Some who survive within the creature can be infected with the seed of Moander. The deity gains knowledge of all those "blessed" with the seed. That connection works both ways, granting the victims a brief look into the god's mind. Moander can cast any spells it knows through any of the seeded victims. Each enslaved victim shares their mind with the deity, making the Abomination permanently smarter and wiser. This avatar is vulnerable to fire due to flammable gasses and fumes that the giant carcass constantly produces. Smaller sources of magical or mundane flames can damage the creature very little and are quickly snuffed out by the Abomination's wet oozing body. Bigger sources of flame, such as dragon's breath, can detonate the Abomination, instantly destroying the avatar in a colossal blaze. The cold is harmful to it, damaging it and halting the rotting. Moander's core can move between piles of filth of big enough size through exuding a relatively small flying egg-shaped pod. These pods contain the essence of Moander and allow it to possess another rotting body, creating a new Abomination. Given enough putrefied matter, the Jawed God's avatar can vomit a shambling mound twice per day and a gibbering mouther once every three days. These spawns are under the god's control for the one-to-twelve following days. After that, the creatures are granted autonomy and they wander away from the creator. Lastly, the Abomination can open a gate at will, sacrificing about a month's worth of rot that sustains it. During cold months, the Abomination of Moander retreats to warm lands or into lava-filled hot cavers of the Underdark, where it is fed and guarded by the dread god's clergy.
Divine Realm: Moander's divine realm — Offalmound, is located in Rarandreth, the 223rd abyssal layer, both in the Great Wheel and the World Tree cosmology. Adherents of the latter worldview speculate that with the deity's demise his realm is either pushed outside the Astral Plane without any connections remaining or collapsed altogether.
Relationships: Moander especially revels in corrupting, enslaving, and rotting beholders and similar creatures. Sages think that to be tied to ancient rivalry with fellow god Bane, while others think that it is due to Moander's ancient bitter enemy Phalse, who resembles a monstrous beholder with a single eye in the center and mouths in place of smaller eyes. Another ancient enemy of Moander's is Tyranthraxus the Possessing Spirit, who, in the days of antiquity, attempted to take over the Jawed God's hold in the Realms. Among gods, Moander has several allies and significantly more foes. Unlike Ghaunadaur, Lolth is an enemy of Moander who lusts after its portfolio. Many of the elven pantheon oppose dark gods, putting them at odds with Moander. This includes Corellon Larethian, Hanali Celanil Rillifane Rallathil, and Solonor Thelandira. The halfling deities Arvoreen and Sheela Peryroyl consider Moander their deadly foe. The Darkbringer gained many bitter rivals among the gods of Netheril, the feuds that lasted for millennia. These ancient foes included Jannath—an aspect of Chauntea, Jergal, Mystryl—the goddess of magic, Selûne, Targus—aspect of Garagos, and the goddess of luck Tyche, who eventually fell by the Darkbringer's scheme. However, Moander made allies of Kozah—ancient aspect of Talos, with whom, Moander sought to destroy anything that Mystryl had a hand in creating. Shar became allied with both Moander and Kozah against her sister Selûne.
Worshipers: Moander's presence and worship have been chronicled in many ancient texts. Some are older than his first recorded organized worship in Netheril. Moanderite worship is predatory dogma that preys on lonely folk adrift in the world. Those desperate enough to join worship welcome the firm direction it gives their life. Moander has never been flush with worshipers, however numerous cults have been dedicated to the deity. Individuals who join Darkbringer's clergy are put through a ceremony where a seed of Moander is planted inside their bodies. The godly seed grows inside, slowly turning the entirety of their insides into rotting plant matter and eventually dried dead greenery. The clergy of Moander is identifiable by a small flowering tendril protruding from the ear and wound through the hair. This seed allows the god directly assume control of any creature infected by it.
Non-Human Worshipers: Moander is served by and can manifest itself as several intelligent non-human creatures, such as algoids, dark trees, gibbering mouthers, shambling mounds, and vegepygmies created by russet mold. Moander and his cultists use giant toads, and giant slugs, for their nefarious purposes, and the deity summons its loyal black or green dragons to serve the Mouth of Moander. The Jawed God's hate of beholders leads to the deity transforming dead enslaved aberrations into rotting death tyrants, fully subservient to it. In the late-14th century DR, Moander received worship from some of wild elves who stood in fear of encroaching civilization. These elves believed that the god of decay could protect them from farmers, ranchers, and loggers.
Places of Worship: Typical temples of the Rotting God are constructed as sprawling underground complexes or atop sharp hills away from prying eyes in the secluded wilderness. The temples are marked by circled of sharp fang-shaped rocks arranged in the shape of Moander's open jaws, surrounding an altar. The underground temples can be found in places with rot, waste, and decaying sewage. The temple complexes' walls are carved with delicate images of elves frowning trees, tortured humanoids, and people being melted by dragons' acid. The oldest place of Moanderite worship in Faerûn was an underground temple known as the Abyss of the Abomination, in the city of Yûlash in the Moonsea region. The temple complex was over 1,000 years old by the 14th century DR. Another shrine of note was the Hill of Fangs, outside the city of Westgate. The hilltop was surrounded by a ring of eight plinths of red stone that resembled curved inward fangs. More obscure places of worship were mere rumors to most. The forests outside of Ylraphon were rumored to shelter shrines of several evil powers, including the worship site called the House of Moander. Another temple of Moander could be found proudly standing in the City of a Thousand Temples—Bezantur in Thay. Following the Jawed God's death during the Time of Troubles, the main well-hidden active place of worship was the Hidden Glades temple by the town of Torsch in Chondalwood. The faith was led by the Mouth of Moander Dalchatha Maereegh. She ran a wide spy network and guided cultists to capture, slay, and rot enemies of the church, turning them into new bodies for Moander to turn into Abominations.
Holy Days: Cultists of Moander are expected to perform a daily ceremonial kill of a creature or gather vegetation to spread rot and decay. Balefire is one of the very few celebrations of the god's worshipers. It takes place on the first of Hammer when Moanderites construct huge bonfires in the name of the god of rot to hold back the cold.
History: A Netherese crowd running from the Abomination of Moander. In the days of ancient Netheril, a common belief was that Moander came to Toril and established his greatest temple in the mountains of Moander's Footsteps to annihilate an elder race, long forgotten even in the days of antiquity. The rotting god poisoned the race's food and water, causing their extinction. Although the deity's origins have never been made clear, Moander appeared throughout some of Faerûn's earliest historical recordings and folklore. Moander was one of the players in the Dawn Cataclysm, Lathander's ill-fated attempt to reshape the Faerûnian pantheon in his own image. Several deities were killed in the events that followed, including the goddess Murdane. However, the biggest loss for Lathander was Tyche, his lover at the time. She refused to partake in Lathander's grab for power and left him to wander the Realms. During that time, she came across a beautiful rose high in the mountains of Toril. The flower was so perfect that the goddess thought it an apology from her misguided consort. In reality, the flower was a seed of Moander. Tyche tucked the rose in her hair, from whence the flower corrupted and rotted her from the inside. To save her, Selûne was forced to split the goddess of luck, birthing Tymora and Beshaba. In the days of ancient Unther, the royal House of Haelcaunter was known as "the consorts of gods". Untheric deities, such as Moander, Gargauth, Shar, Jergal, and the Seven Lost Gods, indeed consorted with the members of the royal family, tasking them with divine missions and guiding them to prosperity or corruption. Not long before the Year of the Rising Flame, 0 DR, Moander attempted to increase his worship on Toril by taking on a humanoid cowled shape and persuading mortals of the importance of rot in nature, equating itself to Chauntea or Silvanus. The deity positioned itself to appear as a goodly natural force not to be feared. The ploy did not sway many, except a smattering of gullible mortals. Eventually, only those who enjoyed death and corruption remained loyal to the cowled god. During that time, Shar considered Moander to be an upstart rival. In the Year of Clinging Death, 75 DR, Moander's armies of "creeping evil" were unleashed on the elven settlement of Tsornyl. The corrupting forces spread blight through the forests that surrounded the city. The deity's dark influence twisted and mutated every living thing in the vicinity of Tsornyl, including members of its own church. These corrupted creatures were shaped into various unknowable horrors, including deepspawn and rotting shambling mounds. Unable to cleanse nor destroy the created evil, elven High Magic was used to sever the "creeping evil" part of Moander and imprison it within the ruined Tsornyl, later renamed to the dreaded forest of Darkwatch. This act cost 32 elven lives, including two High Mages of Myth Drannor. The loss of power echoed in Moander's diminished influence on Toril. Most elves died swiftly and painfully when the rot set in on House Tsornyl. A small number of older and more powerful individuals managed to flee Moander through a gate to Luernla, an isolated elven island in the Beacon Rocks. Some of the survivors were infected with slow rot and Nueltrara Tsornyl made great sacrifices to purge the corruption from her remaining subjects. However, she unwittingly granted them a unique type of undead existence in the process. In the Year of Unkind Weapons, 171 DR, the Cormanthyr elves of Myth Drannor were engaged in a two-year-war against the deity's avatar in its last remaining major temple, located in what later become the city of Yûlash. The avatar was known as the Abomination of Moander—a huge mass of rotting vegetation and carrion that left the ground void of any living thing in its wake. The Coronal of the City of Song and sixteen of High Mages weaved elven High Magics and cast the binding on the Darkbringer. It sealed the essence of the Abomination beneath the ruins, to be released only by an "unborn child." Most of the priests were slain, yet some cultists fled south, and the church managed to survive. Over the next millennia, they tried to free the Abomination, but to no avail. I saw that battle. Moander puffed up like an overproofed loaf of bread. The dragon spat flame at it. Boooom! Fried dragon and chunks of rotting god rained on the city. Took out a piece of the city wall, the Dhostar warehouses, and a lot of the northwestern slums. That crash shook out this town like a dirty rug. The town's merchant nobles thought a new Flight of Dragons had arrived! — Jamal, Thespian of Westgate Moander's Torillian avatar remained trapped until the Kythorn 5, the Year of the Prince, 1357 DR. Moander's cultists found unlikely allies in a sorceress Cassana, her lich ally Zrie Prakis, the Darkbringer's ancient enemy fiend Phalse, and the Fire Knives assassins. The dark alliance pooled their resources to create a living construct, a "nonborn child," each member of the alliance planned on using the construct for their own purpose. The Jawed God's cultists sought to use it to unleash the Abomination of Moander onto the world once more. Against all odds, the construct was lost to the group and gained sentence, becoming the hero known as Alias. Via manipulation and the compulsory magic of her azure bonds, Alias and her companions were lured to the war-torn town of Yûlash and freed Moander from his ancient prison. The Abomination captured Alias and held her inside its massive rotting body as he grew even bigger, feeding off soldiers, beasts, and trees. Burning with a vengeance, the Abomination made way across Cormanthor towards Myth Drannor, the city of his ancient enemies. The avatar left behind a cleared way in the elven forest later called Moander's Road. Eventually, Moander's avatar was destroyed in the aerial battle over Westgate by a red dragon Mistinarperadnacles Hai Draco. Many of the Darkbringer's cultists were killed in the battle of the Hill of Fangs outside of the city by joined forces of Alias, her "brother" Dragonbait, Olive Ruskettle, and Akabar Bel Akash. Of course, the cultists of Moander were far from gone, but the god itself was reduced to being a mere demipower. The Abomination shed a huge part of its rotting carcass along the route it carved through Cormanthor. Since then, Moander's Road was known for a huge mound that once was part of the creature. It spawned strange previously unseen blossoms all around the dead god. Locals believed that something dangerous was lairing within the rotting mound. Before Moander disappeared from Toril once again, it sent visions to the High Priestess Mogion of Sembia, guiding her to the temple in Yûlash. Mere months after the Abomination's demise, Mogion led her group—the Church of Moander, to the ruined temple. She plotted to open a dimensional door to the Abyss to bring Moander's true form to Faerûn, however Mogion only succeeded in opening a small gate allowing several pseudopods of the deity to pour into the Prime Material. These Bits of Moander, as well as the High Priestess possessed by the rotting god, were defeated by Alias, Dragonbait, and a band of adventurers branded with azure bonds.
Supposed Death: Moander attempted a return to power in the Realms in the Year of Shadows, 1358 DR. The deity tracked down the saurial tribe Dragonbait hailed from and transported them as his slaves into a remote location within the Dalelands — Tarkhaldale. The demipower implanted the seed of Moander into Coral, an old flame and mate of Dragonbait's, turning her into the Mouth of Moander, the High Priest of the Rotting God. Reestablished on the Prime Material plane, Moander infected a powerful beholder Xaran, a Harper agent Kyre, and an army of treants. The Darkbringer's slave saurials were tasked with growing a pile of rot to become a new Abomination, defiling all living things in the Lost Vale, and adding their own eggs to the dreaded god's body. In the advent of the Time of Troubles, Alias, Dragonbait, Finder Wyvernspur — Alias's creator and father, confronted the saurial colony and Moander. Dragonbait was forced to kill his old love Coral as there was nothing left of her but rotting vines on the inside. Finder Wyvernspur and Akabar Bel Akash followed the god into the Abyss and sacrificed their lives, destroying the Darkbringer with a shard of para-elemental ice that powered Finder's Stone. Finder inherited Moander's divinity, with sponsorship from Moander's enemies, goddess of luck Tymora and the House Wyvernspur patron goddess Selûne, and became a demigod in his own right. Sages debated how true was Moander's destruction. His avatars were gone, and his existence in the Abyss was cut short by a mortal with heat from the divine. Some claimed to have encountered Moander's body floating in the Astral Plane, and there was evidence of a fraction of the Darkbringer's essence growing in power in the planes. The truth was that Finder didn't succeed at truly killing Moander. Like many other divine beings, Moander was more than a single entity. The old god's consciousness remained in Darkwatch, where it drained power and gained strength from people visiting the place, and one creature of sufficient strength, like an avatar or a Chosen, would be enough for him to regain his demigod status. The method by which he lured people to Darkwatch was by infecting those with special spores. These spores could straightforwardly eat people or influence them like through suggestion to make the infected send more to be infected. Another method by which he lured people to Darkwatch was by making them appear like one of religious significance. Remaining worshipers of Moander received mental whispers from the god, the so-called "Moander dreams". This was met with different degrees of success. Clerics of Cyric ventured there to relish the dark energy there while drow following Vhaeraun wanted to have nothing to do with the place. Meanwhile, the worship of Moander became splintered between cultists who followed the Jawed God and those who embraced a new religion dedicated to rot and corruption. The drow deity Lolth felt vulnerable after the Godswar and quickly seized the opportunity to claim Moander's name as her aspect in the surface world and the Rotting God's hegemony, unclaimed by Finder. Under Moander's guise, Lolth attracted surface humans, elves, and half-elves who found rot and corruption more appealing and comprehensible than Lolth's dogma among the drow. In the Year of Lightning Storms, 1374 DR, strange fog started appearing in the High Forest. All living beings who found themselves within the roaming clouds were turned into rotting mummies adorned with Moander's holy symbol. During the same period of time, a band of Moanderite cultists uncovered ancient, powerful Netherese magics and attempted to use them to rob Finder Wyvernspur of his divine spark in order to return Moander to Toril. The attempt, evidently, was unsuccessful.
Return to Toril: Following the return of dead gods and Toril's healing from the damage done by the Spellplague. Mystra's resurrection heralded the Second Sundering in the 15th century DR. Despite not being fully dead, Moander's influence was returned to the Prime Material plane. The deity laid low, gathering power, hiding in patches of rot, death, and decay, as well as corrupt minds of mortals, such as the Rotting Man of Talona. In the 15th century DR, Moander found influence among foolish mortals seeking power. The god of decay offered pacts to warlocks in exchange for spreading rot, fear, and reverence of the Jawed God. The deity stove the decay of the seeds of Moander and mandated the followers to spread the seeds among individuals of power and influence in the Realms. Moander's return was fueled by him devouring and destroying several gods returned to life during the Second Sundering. One of the deities consumed by the god of rot was Kiputytto, the demigoddess of poison, sister of Loviatar, the Maiden of Pain. Flush with stolen divine power, Moander was opposed by the Chosen who secretly sought to stop his quest for power. One victory against returning the god of decay to prominence was the Chosen deceiving Moander into breaking his alliance with Shar.
Rumors and Legends:
• Brindul Alley in Waterdeep is haunted by a strange flying hand that greatly resembles the holy symbol of Moander. There are many theories of the hand's origin. However, none are confirmed. • Citadel of Fungi in the vicinity of Moander's Road is known for copious amounts of yellow-green mold and fungus in the 15th century DR. The ancient citadel's treasures remain un-plundered as locals whisper of Moander's influence spreading from the long-killed Abomination, rotting underneath a hill. • Many rumors about gods circulate among mortals. The most salacious are stories of Mystra's divine lovers. There have been claims of Azuth, Helm, Shar, Bane, Moander, or the nearest rock to consort with the goddess of magic. The truthfulness of all these claims is not known.
Source: Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn p. 280

monster.name: Swanmay [5.5e]
monster.speed: Walk 30 ft., Fly 40 ft. (swan form only)

trait.name: Gear
trait.text: Longbow, Scimitar.

trait.name: Flyby (Swan Form Only)
trait.text: The swanmay doesn't provoke an Opportunity Attack action when it flies out of an enemy's reach.

action.name: Multiattack
action.text: The swanmay makes two attacks, using Beak, Longbow, or Scimitar in any combination.

action.name: Beak (Swan Form Only)
action.text: Melee Attack Roll: +6, reach 5 ft. Hit: 7 (1d6+4) Piercing damage. If the target is a Large or smaller creature, it has the Prone condition.

action.name: Scimitar (Humanoid Form Only)
action.text: Melee Attack Roll: +6, reach 5 ft. Hit: 11 (2d6+4) Slashing damage.

action.name: Longbow (Humanoid Form Only)

action.name: Shape-Shift (Bonus Action)

monster.description:
A swanmay is a humanoid that can transform into a swan, via an induced form of lycanthropy.
Description: Swanmays are intelligent rangers (or druids) that can take the form of swans, mostly for mobility purposes. In humanoid form, they resemble beautiful women, often wearing light armor or attendant garb. The swan form gives some advantages in combat, but mainly improves communication with natural beings. As swanmays become more experienced, they can charm people, and speak with animals, as well as with plants. The most experienced swanmays can charm monsters and even gain a high resistance to weapons other than cold iron, which applies to both forms.
Behavior: These induced lycanthropes keep themselves to their own kind, never divulging about their true nature. They dislike noisy, ferocious, and evil beings.
Combat: In swan form, the creature takes reduced damage except against cold iron and has higher resistance to magical spells. In this form, they attack with flying leaps, buffeting their wings, and biting. In human form, they fight in light armor, and attack with swords and daggers at close range, and bows at long range.
Society: Such creatures are part of a secret order that wishes to protect the wilderness from evil. Only good-willed females are permitted to join the order, and must have history in protecting the wild. The order has additional requirements for recruits, such as being able to speak Sylvan and the ability to speak with animals. As well as meeting these requirements, an initiate must perform a great deed for another swanmay before being accepted into the order. When they are officially a part of the order, they accept a feathered token that allows them to change forms. The token can also be a signet ring or a feathered garment.
Homelands: Swanmays rarely travel outside a specific area, as they prefer living in sororities near rivers, lakes, and forests teeming with wildlife. Some can be found across the forests of Cormanthor. They are known to be found in the freshwater rivers and lakes of the Moonshae Isles, where the Swanmay River winds across the island of Alaron. There are legends of the Seven Swanmays who live in the King's Forest of Cormyr, granting good fortune to those who revere and protect life and nature of the woods, and bringing misfortune on those who endanger the forest with fires and poaches.
Beyond the Prime Material plane, swanmays can be found in the Beastlands.
Relationships: Swanmays get on well with like-minded forest dwellers, such as dryads and wood elves.
History: The first swanmay was a human ranger named Fionnghuala. Fionnghuala gave her life defending King Oberon of the Seelie Court from the Queen of Air and Darkness. In reward for her selfless bravery and sacrifice, Oberon raised her from the dead and made her a demigod, while his wife Titania offered her the magic white feather that transformed her into a part-fey being and made her into a swanmay.
Notable Swanmays • Albaeryl Tanthlyn • Dathae of Essembra • Fionnghuala • Lharave
Source: Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn p. 281

monster.name: Werewyvern [5.5e]
monster.speed: Walk 30 ft., Fly 40 ft. (wyvern or hybrid form only)
monster.languages: Common, Draconic (can't speak in wyvern form)

trait.name: Gear
trait.text: 6 Javelins.

trait.name: Flyby (Wyvern or Hybrid Form Only)
trait.text: The werewyvern doesn't provoke an Opportunity Attack action when it flies out of an enemy's reach.

action.name: Multiattack
action.text: The werewyvern makes three attacks, using Javelin or Rend in any combination. It can replace one of these attacks with one Stinger attack.

action.name: Javelin (Humanoid or Hybrid Form Only)
action.text: Melee or Ranged Attack Roll: +7, reach 5 ft. or range 30/120 ft. Hit: 18 (4d6+4) Piercing damage.

action.name: Rend
action.text: Melee Attack Roll: +7, reach 5 ft. Hit: 18 (4d6+4) Slashing damage.

action.name: Stinger (Wyvern or Hybrid Form Only)
action.text: Melee Attack Roll: +7, reach 5 ft. Hit: 7 (1d6+4) Piercing damage plus 16 (3d10) Poison damage, and the target has the Poisoned condition until the start of the werewyvern's next turn. If the target is a Humanoid, it is subjected to the following effect. Constitution Saving Throw: DC 16. Failure: The target is cursed. If the cursed target drops to 0 Hit Points, it instead becomes a Werewyvern under the DM's control and has 20 Hit Points. Success: The target is immune to this werewyvern's curse for 24 hours.

action.name: Shape-Shift (Bonus Action)
action.text: The werewyvern shape-shifts into a Medium wyvern-humanoid hybrid or a Large wyvern, or it returns to its true humanoid form. Its game statistics, other than its size, are the same in each form. Any equipment it is wearing or carrying isn't transformed.

monster.description:
Changed by the Venom of the Wyvern Treasure: Individual
Among the rarest of were-creatures, werewyverns change from their humanoid forms into lean wyverns or into draconic-humanoid hybrids. Most werewyverns possess a draconic greed and ferocity and thus often find work as bandits, mercenaries, or assassins. They are opportunistic warriors and prefer ambushes when possible. Werewyverns like to keep their wyvern form a secret until they need an upper hand in a fight or an aerial escape. Werewyverns transmit lycanthropy through their potent venom. The curse's transmission is unpredictable and often as much a surprise to the werewyvern as it is to the victim.
A werewyvern is a type of lycanthrope that can shapechange into a wyvern. They are the rarest of the werecreatures known to exist as of the turn of the 16th century DR.
Description: As with other lycanthropes, werewyverns have three forms: their normal humanoid form, a lean wyvern form, and a hybrid form combining humanoid and draconic-seeming wyvern traits.
Personality: Werewyverns typically have a vicious nature and a greed akin to that of dragons. They prefer to keep their true nature secret, transforming only when they need to get an advantage on a foe or to fly away.
Abilities: The curse of werewyvern lycanthropy is passed on via their venom. Whether it takes hold or not, however, is unpredictable, making it a surprise to both the victim and the werewyern itself.
Tactics: In battle, a werewyvern favors attacking from ambush and opportunistic strikes. Once transformed, they fight with flyby attacks and use their claws or javelins flung from on high.
Society: Owing to their proclivities, werewyverns operate as assassins, brigands, and mercenaries.
Variations: In addition to the standard variety, there also exist greater werewyverns. The exact differences between the two are not well known due to the rarity of the species. The one known as Ekim Cyre had an inherent resistance against the elements and could not be harmed by non-magical weapons.
History: Werewyverns seemed to be incredibly rare in the Realms. In Cormyr in the mid-to-late 1300s DR, it was said by many locals that a brigand werewyvern, known as Black Shaernauba, would rob travelers. If they tried to fight back, she would assume the form of a wyvern, and fly away with the goods. The werewyvern was said to live in a cave full of riches, and kept attractive men as captives. She was also said to have slain Purple Dragons who tried to make a base near her home, as well as others setting up establishments.
In the Year of the Gauntlet, 1369 DR, a werewyvern by the name of Ekim Cyre, along with a green dragon, protected the Bhaalspawn Abazigal from invaders.
Circa 1501 DR, the Purple Dragons suspected werewyverns were operating on Wyvernfang peak in the Thunder Peaks near High Dale, based on claims of their high intelligence and organization, including herding sheep in valleys only accessible from the sky and building defensive walls. Thus, the Crown proposed sending an ambassador to High Dale; this would be an amethyst-dragon-riding knight who could hunt the wyverns. However, High Dale's High Constable refused each candidate.
At the same time, in the Moonshae Isles, a werewyvern was known to dwell in the marsh of Frostfenn on the isle of Norland. The Purple Dragon Knights came even this far to hunt it.
Notable Werewyverns • Black Shaernauba, a rumored werewyvern in Cormyr. • Ekim Cyre, a greater werewyvern that dwelt in the lair of Abazigal.
Source: Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn p. 284

monster.name: Zhentilar Soldier [5.5e]

trait.name: Gear
trait.text: Leather Armor, Pistol, Shortsword.

action.name: Multiattack
action.text: The Zhentilar makes two attacks, using Shortsword or Pistol in any combination. It can replace one attack with a use of Knock Down.

action.name: Shortsword
action.text: Melee Attack Roll: +4, reach 5 ft. Hit: 5 (1d6+2) Piercing damage plus 2 (1d4) Poison damage.

action.name: Pistol
action.text: Ranged Attack Roll: +4, range 80/320 ft. Hit: 7 (1d10+2) Piercing damage.

action.text: Strength Saving Throw: DC 12, one creature within 5 feet that the Zhentilar can see. Failure: 4 (1d4+2) Bludgeoning damage. If the target is a Medium or smaller creature, it has the Prone condition.

monster.description:
Wardens of the Zhentarim Treasure: Armaments
The Zhentilar is the militant wing of the Zhentarim. Zhentilar forces occupy Zhentarim strongholds such as Zhentil Keep and Darkhold and defend these places from the Zhentarim's many enemies. If the Zhentarim is one big family, then the Zhentilar are the protective older siblings who look out for their kin. Zhentilar also conduct other important organizational work such as safeguarding powerful magic items or escorting Zhentarim leaders.
Zhentilar Soldier: Zhentilar soldiers occupy Zhentarim fortresses and outposts. The price of betraying the organization is so steep that many Zhentilar soldiers would rather die for the Zhentarim than abandon their post.
The Zhentilar are the standing military force of Zhentil Keep and the enforcement arm of the Zhentarim (the "Black Network"). Serving as both ruthless conquerors and elite sellswords, they operate across Faerûn from the Moonsea to the Sword Coast. Their lore centers on tyranny, elite mercenary work, and shadow politics.
History and Origins: • Foundation: Formed after the death of the warlord Zhentar in 753 DR, the Zhentilar were officially expanded into a full army following the devastating "Night Plague" in 882 DR. • The Black Network: In 1261 DR, the wizard Manshoon founded the Zhentarim. The Zhentilar became the primary military and enforcement arm for this mercantile and espionage organization. • The Citadel of the Raven: Along with Zhentil Keep itself, the Zhentilar maintained a massive fortress called the Citadel of the Raven. • Fall and Rebirth: During the 15th century, the Zhentarim evolved from an overt military-nation into a continental network of elite mercenaries.
Key Figures and Lore Icons • Manshoon: The founder of the Zhentarim, a brilliant but fiercely ambitious wizard who controlled Zhentil Keep alongside a triumvirate of leaders. • Fzoul Chembryl: The High Priest of Bane, who ultimately took over the Black Network, transforming it into a formidable faith-based organization. • The Pereghost: The shadowy undead commander of the mercenary fortress of Darkhold. He transformed the Zhentilar's reputation from backstabbing thugs to highly disciplined, professional mercenaries. • Scyllua Darkhope: A high-ranking champion of Bane and Castellan of Zhentil Keep, responsible for the city's day-to-day defenses.
Equipment and Combat Style • The Iron Guard: Zhentilar soldiers are typically clad in heavy, distinctive black plate armor and are well-known for utilizing state-of-the-art weaponry, and occasionally banned contraband like poisons or smokepowder weapons. • The Naug-orls: Also known as "Devil Worms," this was a specialized, covert division of the Zhentilar containing assassins, spies, and thieves who operated as a secret police within the Keep.
Adventure Hooks • Contracted Muscle: Your party might encounter a squad of four elite Zhentilar soldiers (led by a Sternhelm) offering their services as caravan guards for 20 gold pieces per day. • Sabotage and Ransom: Historically, Zhentarim agents have been known to stir up local monster populations or capture castles to force isolated towns and kingdoms to rely on the Zhentilar for protection. • The Black Road: Adventurers can find themselves tangling with Zhentilar forces who routinely extort trade routes or harass independent operators who refuse to pay the Zhentarim protection fees.
Source: Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn p. 285

monster.description:
Wardens of the Zhentarim Treasure: Armaments

If the Zhentarim is one big family, then the Zhentilar are the protective older siblings who look out for their kin. Zhentilar also conduct other important organizational work such as safeguarding powerful magic items or escorting Zhentarim leaders.
Zhentilar Paladin of Bane: The Zhentilar's most-respected commanders and sergeants tend to be spellswords or holy warriors who worship nefarious higher powers, such as Bane.
The Zhentilar are the elite military forces of the Zhentarim (the Black Network), serving as the brutal, organized arm of Bane, the god of tyranny, fear, and hatred. Paladins who pledge themselves to Bane through the Zhentilar are sworn to establish rigid order, ruthlessly crush chaos, and ensure that the strong dominate the weak.
The Core Lore: • The Patron: Bane (The Black Lord/The Black Hand) demands absolute discipline, strife to weed out the weak, and careful orchestration of control rather than senseless slaughter. • The Black Network: The Zhentarim spans across Faerûn, converting political influence, trading networks, and mercenary might into holy conquests for Bane. • The Order: Zhentilar Paladins (sometimes known as part of the Knights of the Black Gauntlet) enforce law via tyranny. They view their cause as bringing necessary order and structure to a chaotic world, believing peace comes only through total subjugation.
Roleplaying a Zhentilar Paladin: • The Oath: Unlike good-aligned paladins, they usually follow the Oath of Conquest, emphasizing martial prowess, fear as a weapon, and the rule of the strong. • Alignment: Lawful Evil. They loathe chaotic villains (like typical bandits) just as much as heroes, believing that chaos undermines the supreme, structured society they are trying to build. • Motivations: They operate as high-ranking enforcers, generals, or regional warlords, often infiltrating frontier towns to manipulate local militias or taking over thieves' guilds to install themselves as the iron-fisted ruling class.
Campaign Adventures in Faerûn: • Moonsea Hegemony: Zhentilar Paladins are heavily embedded in the Moonsea region, historically operating out of Zhentil Keep, the Citadel of the Raven, and Mulmaster. They frequently clash with the Harpers and the Lords' Alliance. • The Western Heartlands: Since the devastation of Zhentil Keep, the Black Network's center of power shifted to Darkhold. Adventures here involve covertly bribing nobles, running slave camps, and violently suppressing rebellions. • Icewind Dale: Zhentarim influence (and Zhentilar mercenaries) stretches all the way to Ten Towns. They can serve as dangerous puppet-masters, such as the town speakers Naerth Maxildanarr, creating local conflicts to secure trade monopolies.
The Zhentalir: The Zhentilar are the standing military force of Zhentil Keep and the enforcement arm of the Zhentarim (the "Black Network"). Serving as both ruthless conquerors and elite sellswords, they operate across Faerûn from the Moonsea to the Sword Coast. Their lore centers on tyranny, elite mercenary work, and shadow politics.

monster.name: Biha Babir [5.5e]
monster.speed: Walk 30 ft., Fly 60 ft., Swim 90 ft.

trait.name: Amphibious
trait.text: Biha Babir can breathe air and water.

trait.name: Elemental Restoration
trait.text: If Biha Babir dies outside the Elemental Plane of Water, her body dissolves into brine, and she gains a new body in 1d4 days, reviving with all her Hit Points somewhere on the Plane of Water.

trait.name: Legendary Resistance (3/Day)
trait.text: If Biha Babir fails a saving throw, she can choose to succeed instead.

trait.name: Wishes
trait.text: Biha Babir knows the Wish spell but can cast it only on behalf of a non-genie creature who communicates a wish in a way Biha Babir can understand. If Biha Babir casts the spell for a creature, she suffers none of the spell's stress. Once Biha Babir has cast it three times, she can't do so again for 365 days.

action.name: Multiattack
action.text: Biha Babir makes two Marine Burst attacks. She can replace one of these attacks with a Tail attack.

action.name: Marine Burst
action.text: Melee or Ranged Attack Roll: +10, reach 5 ft. or range 60 ft. Hit: 17 (2d10+6) Cold damage.

action.name: Tail (Marid Form Only)
action.text: Melee Attack Roll: +10, reach 15 ft. Hit: 13 (2d6+6) Bludgeoning damage and if the target is Huge or smaller, it has the Prone condition.

action.name: Spellcasting
action.text:
Biha Babir casts one of the following spells, requiring no Material components and using Charisma as the spellcasting ability (spell save DC 17):
• At will: Create or Destroy Water, Detect Magic, Major Image • 2/day each: Control Water (Flood, Part Water, or Redirect Flow only), Dispel Magic, Invisibility • 1/day each: Control Weather, Plane Shift

action.name: Fluid Form (Bonus Action)
action.text: Biha Babir shape-shifts into a form resembling a Beast or Humanoid that is Medium or smaller, while retaining her game statistics (other than her size), or returns to her true marid form.

legendary.name: Legendary Actions (3/Turn)
legendary.text: Legendary Action Uses: 3/Turn. Immediately after another creature's turn, Biha Babir can expend a use to take one of the following actions. Biha Babir regains all expended uses at the start of each of her turns.

legendary.name: Misty Burst
legendary.text: Biha Babir teleports to an unoccupied space she can see within 30 feet of herself and makes one Marine Burst attack.

legendary.name: Whirlpool
legendary.text: Strength Saving Throw: DC 18, each creature in a 30-foot Emanation originating from Biha Babir. Failure: 10 (3d6) Force damage, and the target is pulled 15 feet straight toward Biha Babir. Success: Half damage only. Failure or Success: Biha Babir can't use this action again until the start of her next turn.

monster.spells: Create or Destroy Water, Detect Magic, Major Image, Control Water, Dispel Magic, Invisibility, Control Weather, Plane Shift
monster.description:
Biha Babir Scheming Marid Ruler
The calculating Biha Babir rules the pelagic city of Maran Saya in Calimshan. Though her physical form is as fluid as the ocean itself, she typically presents as a marid crowned in coral, with her lower half lengthening into a sinewy, eel-like tail.
History: Before becoming ruler of Maran Saya, Biha Babir worked as a spy. She has traveled across Calimshan, infiltrating rival genie courts and eliminating remnants of the Twisted Rune. Some accounts even tell of her fighting alongside Sultana Songal during the Night of Fleeing Shadows. Biha Babir took up leadership of Maran Saya after the previous ruler, her father, retired. People know her as a shrewd ruler, preferring battles of wit over clashes of swords. Of the genie leaders in Calimshan, Biha Babir maintains the strongest spy network, and she is rumored to have informants in every major city of the region. For years, Biha Babir has searched tirelessly for the Calimemnon Crystal (see chapter 8), the legendary prison of the powerful genies Calim and Memnon. She believes obtaining that crystal would allow her to wipe Calimshan off the map and seize control of whatever genie empire rises from the wreckage.
Personality: Biha Babir's demeanor is like the ocean: seemingly placid on the surface, but dangerous and fierce deep below. Her amiable attitude hides a cunning mind. Biha Babir is politically savvy and prefers to outsmart her opponents rather than battle them, though she doesn't shy from combat if necessary. Biha Babir covets opulence, but she also values information and learning just as much as material wealth. Offering valuable information is a surefire way to gain an audience with the her, but those caught lying to her are severely punished.
Biha Babir is a powerful Marid (water genie) and Sultan of Maran Saya — an underwater, crystalline Coral Palace located off the coast of Calimshan in the Forgotten Realms.
The Calimemnon Crystal Conflict: Sultan Biha Babir is best known for his fierce rivalry with Sultana Songal of Calimshan. The core of this conflict revolves around the Calimemnon Crystal, which plummeted into the Calim Desert near Calimport like a "shooting star". Biha Babir actively sought to capture this magical artifact using the power and resources of Maran Saya, putting him in direct opposition to Songal's agents who were tasked with securing it for Calimshan.
Threat and Lore: Biha Babir is a giant genie possessing immense magical strength and the ability to manipulate water and elemental magic. As a Marid, he commands the deep ocean environments and leads an army or network of aquatic agents from Maran Saya.
Source: Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn p. 252

monster.name: Karas Chembryl [5.5e]

trait.name: Gear
trait.text: Studded Leather Armor.

trait.name: Evasion
trait.text: If Karas is subjected to an effect that allows her to make a Dexterity saving throw to take only half damage, Karas instead takes no damage if she succeeds on the save and only half damage if she fails. She can't use this trait if she has the Incapacitated condition.

trait.name: Legendary Resistance (3/Day or 4/Day in Lair)
trait.text: If Karas fails a saving throw, she can choose to succeed instead.

action.name: Multiattack
action.text: Karas makes two attacks using Dread Dagger or Tyrant's Blade in any combination.

action.name: Dread Dagger
action.text: Melee or Ranged Attack Roll: +8, reach 5 ft. or range 20/60 ft. Hit: 10 (2d4+5) Piercing damage plus 4 (1d8) Necrotic damage. Hit or Miss: The dagger magically returns to Karas's hand immediately after a ranged attack.

action.name: Tyrant's Blade
action.text: Melee Attack Roll: +8, reach 5 ft. Hit: 8 (1d6+5) Slashing damage and the target has the Frightened condition until the start of Karas's next turn. If the target is already Frightened, it instead takes 10 (3d6) Psychic damage.

action.name: Spellcasting
action.text:
Karas casts one of the following spells, requiring no Material components and using Intelligence as the spellcasting ability (spell save DC 15, +7 to hit with spell attacks):
• At will: Friends, Silence, Thaumaturgy • 2/day: Ray of Sickness (level 5 version) • 1/day: Blight, Mislead

action.name: Withdraw (Bonus Action)
action.text: Karas moves up to half her Speed without provoking Opportunity Attack action and takes the Hide action.

legendary.name: Legendary Actions (4/Turn)
legendary.text: Legendary Action Uses: 3/Turn (4/Turn in Lair) Immediately after another creature's turn, Karas can expend a use to take one of the following actions. Karas regains all expended uses at the start of each of their turns.

legendary.name: Harrow
legendary.text: Wisdom Saving Throw: DC 15, one creature Karas can see within 90 feet of herself. Failure: 10 (3d6) Psychic damage, and the target has the Frightened condition for 1 minute. While Frightened, the target's Speed is 0 feet, and it repeats the save at the end of each of its turns, ending the effect on a success. Failure or Success: Karas can't take this action again until the start of her next turn.

legendary.name: Stealth Attack
legendary.text: Karas makes one Dread Dagger attack and uses Withdraw.

legendary.name: Karas Lair
legendary.text:
Karas extends her connection to the Dead Three into the region she inhabits, creating the following effects:
• Creeping Dread: Terror runs rampant in Karas's domain. Within 1 mile of the lair, creatures other than members of the Zhentarim and cultists of Bane, Bhaal, or Myrkul have Disadvantage on saving throws to avoid or end the Frightened condition.
• Death's Lore: When a Humanoid dies within 1 mile of the lair, Karas learns one secret that the Humanoid knew.
If Karas dies or moves her lair elsewhere, these effects end immediately.

monster.spells: Friends, Silence, Thaumaturgy, Ray of Sickness, Blight, Mislead
monster.description:
Karas Chembryl: Assassin Heir to a Sinister Legacy After the death of patriarch Foul Chembryl, House Chembryl and its descendants were scattered across Faerün. Some members have dutifully continued the family's dedication to Bane, while others have sought to free themselves from that god's malignant shadow. However, none have embraced the Chembryls' tyrannical legacy more than Karas Chembryl, a ruthless assassin whose devotion to the gods Bane, Bhaal, and Myrkul has earned her the title Auspice of the Dead Three.
History: Karas was born to a distant branch of the Chembryl family living in Waterdeep. Though that side of the family had long since abandoned service of Bane, Karas began to exhibit signs of that god's blessing: a callous silver-tongue, an unnaturally intimidating presence, and an affinity for occult magic. Out of fear, Karas's parents discouraged her from using her gifts, hiding their family's history and pressuring the girl toward a pretense of normalcy. Restless and dissatisfied with her life, Karas fell in league with the Zhentarim. When her surname sparked recognition among the elder Zhents, she began researching her lineage, eventually uncovering the stories of Foul Chembryl. Karas grew furious at her family for hiding the truth and embraced her gifts as a scion of Bane. Within a few years, Karas became a fearsome assassin and high-ranking member of the Zhentarim. Her travels across Faerün led her to uncover Bane's relationship with Bhaal and Myrkul. Feeling kinship with the off-maligned gods, Karas pledged herself to the Dead Three. She now operates primarily out of Baldur's Gate, where she strives to uncover remnants of Bane, Bhaal, and Myrkul's might hidden in and around the bustling city.
Personality: Ruthless and fiercely independent, Karas craves power in all its forms. She wields her words with the same cunning as she does her blades, frequently luring opponents into underestimating her before striking unseen. Though she is a member of the Zhentarim, Karas cares little for the organization's hierarchy and family dynamics. Karas views leadership of the Zhentarim as her birthright and hopes that, by amassing power from the Dead Three, she can one day overthrow the Pereghost, the leader of the Zhentarim, and claim what is rightfully hers.
Karas Chembryl is an assassin heiress and a malignant force in the city of Baldur's Gate. Heavily tied to dark, region-specific cabals, she is a deadly villain.
Her prominent backstory and mechanics include: • Bloodline: She is the daughter of Fzoul Chembryl, the formidable high cleric of Bane and a legendary figure of evil within Faerûn's history. • Lore snippet: She is a manipulator of ancient, buried secrets and an assassin connected to the deadly machinations throughout the Sword Coast
Source: Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn p. 263
